questions.question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{2}\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1})(\sqrt{x^{4}+x^{2}+1})}dx$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{2}\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1})(\sqrt{x^{4}+x^{2}+1})}dx$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_html:
$I=\int_{0}^{2}[\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{4}+x^{2}+1})}]dx$

$\begin{aligned} & =\int_{0}^{2}⎡⎣⎢\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{4}+2x^{2}+1-x^{2}})}⎤⎦⎥dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}⎡⎣⎢\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot (\sqrt{(x^{2}+1)^{2}-x^{2}})}⎤⎦⎥dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}⎡⎣⎢\frac{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot {\sqrt{(x^{2}+1+x)(x^{2}+1-x)}}]}⎤⎦⎥dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}⎡⎣⎢\frac{(\sqrt{x}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1})}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{2}+1+x}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{2}+1-x})}⎤⎦⎥dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}⎡⎣⎢\frac{\sqrt{x}}{(\sqrt{x+1}) \cdot (\sqrt{x^{2}-x+1})}⎤⎦⎥dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}[\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{(x+1)(x^{2}-x+1)}}]dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}[\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{3}+1}}]dx \end{aligned}$

Let $x=t^{2} \Rightarrow dx=2tdt$

$I=\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}[\frac{2t^{2}}{\sqrt{t^{6}+1}}]dt=(\frac{2}{3})\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}[\frac{3t^{2}}{\sqrt{t^{6}+1}}]dt$

Let $t^{3}=u \Rightarrow 3t^{2}dt=du$

$I=(\frac{2}{3})^{2} \cdot \int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}}[\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^{2}+1}}]$

Using standard integration formulaes :

$\int (\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}})dx=ln|x+\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}|+C$

= $(\frac{2}{3}) \cdot [ln|u+\sqrt{u^{2}+1}|]_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}}$

$=(\frac{2}{3}) \cdot [ln(2\sqrt{2}+3)-ln1]=(\frac{2}{3}) \cdot [ln(3+2\sqrt{2})]$

questions.question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}})dx$ is :
questions.question_html: The value of the integral $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}})dx$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}}dx$ We will use the standard property: If $I=\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx,$ then $I=\int_{-a}^{a}f(-x)dx$ and hence $2I=\int_{-a}^{a}(f(x)+f(-x))dx$ Now here, $f(x)=\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}}$ So, $f(-x)=\frac{32cos^{4}(-x)}{1+e^{sin(-x)}}$ Using $cos(-x)=cosx$ and $sin(-x)=-sinx$ , $f(-x)=\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{-sinx}}$ Therefore, $f(x)+f(-x)=32cos^{4}x(\frac{1}{1+e^{sinx}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{-sinx}})$ Now simplify the bracket: $\frac{1}{1+e^{sinx}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{-sinx}}$ Let $t=e^{sinx}$ . Then $e^{-sinx}=\frac{1}{t}$ . So, $\frac{1}{1+t}+\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{t}}=\frac{1}{1+t}+\frac{t}{1+t}=1$ Hence, $f(x)+f(-x)=32cos^{4}x$ So, $2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}32cos^{4}xdx$ Thus, $I=16\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}cos^{4}xdx$ Since $cos^{4}x$ is an even function, $I=32\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}cos^{4}xdx$ Now use the identity $cos^{4}x=(cos^{2}x)^{2}=(\frac{1+cos2x}{2})^{2}$ which gives $cos^{4}x=\frac{3+4cos2x+cos4x}{8}$ Therefore, $I=32\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{3+4cos2x+cos4x}{8}dx$ $I=4\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3+4cos2x+cos4x)dx$ Now integrate termwise: $\int 3dx=3x,\int 4cos2xdx=2sin2x,\int cos4xdx=\frac{sin4x}{4}$ So, $I=4[3x+2sin2x+\frac{sin4x}{4}]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}$ At $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , $3x=\frac{3\pi}{4},sin2x=sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1,sin4x=sin\pi=0$ At $x=0$ , $3x=0,sin0=0$ Hence, $I=4(\frac{3\pi}{4}+2)$ $I=3\pi+8$ So the correct answer is: $3\pi+8$ Hence, Option B is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}}dx$

We will use the standard property:

If

$I=\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx,$

then

$I=\int_{-a}^{a}f(-x)dx$

and hence

$2I=\int_{-a}^{a}(f(x)+f(-x))dx$

Now here,

$f(x)=\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{sinx}}$

So,

$f(-x)=\frac{32cos^{4}(-x)}{1+e^{sin(-x)}}$

Using $cos(-x)=cosx$ and $sin(-x)=-sinx$ ,

$f(-x)=\frac{32cos^{4}x}{1+e^{-sinx}}$

Therefore,

$f(x)+f(-x)=32cos^{4}x(\frac{1}{1+e^{sinx}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{-sinx}})$

Now simplify the bracket:

$\frac{1}{1+e^{sinx}}+\frac{1}{1+e^{-sinx}}$

Let $t=e^{sinx}$ . Then $e^{-sinx}=\frac{1}{t}$ . So,

$\frac{1}{1+t}+\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{t}}=\frac{1}{1+t}+\frac{t}{1+t}=1$

Hence,

$f(x)+f(-x)=32cos^{4}x$

So,

$2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}32cos^{4}xdx$

Thus,

$I=16\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}cos^{4}xdx$

Since $cos^{4}x$ is an even function,

$I=32\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}cos^{4}xdx$

Now use the identity

$cos^{4}x=(cos^{2}x)^{2}=(\frac{1+cos2x}{2})^{2}$

which gives

$cos^{4}x=\frac{3+4cos2x+cos4x}{8}$

Therefore,

$I=32\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{3+4cos2x+cos4x}{8}dx$

$I=4\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3+4cos2x+cos4x)dx$

Now integrate termwise:

$\int 3dx=3x,\int 4cos2xdx=2sin2x,\int cos4xdx=\frac{sin4x}{4}$

So,

$I=4[3x+2sin2x+\frac{sin4x}{4}]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}$

At $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ ,

$3x=\frac{3\pi}{4},sin2x=sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1,sin4x=sin\pi=0$

At $x=0$ ,

$3x=0,sin0=0$

Hence,

$I=4(\frac{3\pi}{4}+2)$

$I=3\pi+8$

So the correct answer is:

$3\pi+8$

Hence, Option B is correct.

questions.question_text: If $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=1+i\sqrt{2}$ , where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ are two roots of the equation $x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=0,a,b, \in ℝ$ , then $\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx$ is equal to:
questions.question_html:
If $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=1+i\sqrt{2}$ , where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ are two roots of the equation

$x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=0,a,b, \in ℝ$ , then $\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Since the coefficients $a,b,c$ are real, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs. Given two roots are: $\alpha=1,\beta=1+i\sqrt{2}$ So the third root must be: $1-i\sqrt{2}$ Hence the cubic polynomial is: $x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=(x-1)(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))$ Now first multiply the conjugate factors: $(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))$ This is of the form: $(A-iB)(A+iB)=A^{2}+B^{2}$ with $A=x-1,B=\sqrt{2}$ So, $(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))=(x-1)^{2}+2$ Therefore, $x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=(x-1)((x-1)^{2}+2)$ Let $y=x-1$ . Then: $(x-1)((x-1)^{2}+2)=(x-1)^{3}+2(x-1)$ Now expand: $(x-1)^{3}=x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x-1$ So, $x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x-1+2x-2$ $=x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3$ Now evaluate: $\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx=\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3)dx$ Using symmetry: $x^{3}$ is an odd function, so $\int_{-1}^{1}x^{3}dx=0$ $5x$ is also odd, so $\int_{-1}^{1}5xdx=0$ Thus, $\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3)dx=\int_{-1}^{1}(-3x^{2}-3)dx$ Now, $\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}dx=[\frac{x^{3}}{3}]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{1}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3})=\frac{2}{3}$ Therefore, $\int_{-1}^{1}(-3x^{2})dx=-3 \cdot \frac{2}{3}=-2$ Also, $\int_{-1}^{1}(-3)dx=-3(2)=-6$ So total value: $-2-6=-8$ Hence, $\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx=-8$ The correct option is: $-8$ So, Option C is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Since the coefficients $a,b,c$ are real, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs.

Given two roots are:

$\alpha=1,\beta=1+i\sqrt{2}$

So the third root must be:

$1-i\sqrt{2}$

Hence the cubic polynomial is:

$x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=(x-1)(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))$

Now first multiply the conjugate factors:

$(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))$

This is of the form:

$(A-iB)(A+iB)=A^{2}+B^{2}$

with

$A=x-1,B=\sqrt{2}$

So,

$(x-(1+i\sqrt{2}))(x-(1-i\sqrt{2}))=(x-1)^{2}+2$

Therefore,

$x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=(x-1)((x-1)^{2}+2)$

Let $y=x-1$ . Then:

$(x-1)((x-1)^{2}+2)=(x-1)^{3}+2(x-1)$

Now expand:

$(x-1)^{3}=x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x-1$

So,

$x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c=x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x-1+2x-2$

$=x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3$

Now evaluate:

$\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx=\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3)dx$

Using symmetry:

  • $x^{3}$ is an odd function, so

$\int_{-1}^{1}x^{3}dx=0$

  • $5x$ is also odd, so

$\int_{-1}^{1}5xdx=0$

Thus,

$\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}-3x^{2}+5x-3)dx=\int_{-1}^{1}(-3x^{2}-3)dx$

Now,

$\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}dx=[\frac{x^{3}}{3}]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{1}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3})=\frac{2}{3}$

Therefore,

$\int_{-1}^{1}(-3x^{2})dx=-3 \cdot \frac{2}{3}=-2$

Also,

$\int_{-1}^{1}(-3)dx=-3(2)=-6$

So total value:

$-2-6=-8$

Hence,

$\int_{-1}^{1}(x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c)dx=-8$

The correct option is:

$-8$

So, Option C is correct.

questions.explanation_html:

questions.question_text: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36}f(\frac{tx}{36})dt=4\alpha f(x)$ . If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4,\beta)$ , then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.question_html: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36}f(\frac{tx}{36})dt=4\alpha f(x)$ . If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4,\beta)$ , then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\int_{0}^{36}f(\frac{tx}{36})dt=4\alpha f(x)$ Let $\frac{tx}{36}=u \Rightarrow \frac{x}{36}dt=du$ $\int_{0}^{x}f(u)\frac{36}{x}du=4\alpha f(x)$ Integration is w.r.t $u$ , so treat $x$ as a constant $\int_{0}^{x}f(u)du=\frac{4x}{36}\alpha f(x)=\frac{x}{9}\alpha f(x)$ Now, differentiate both sides w.r.t $x$ , use Leibniz theorem in LHS: $1 \cdot f(x)=\frac{\alpha}{9}[1 \cdot f(x)+xf^{'}(x)]$ $\Rightarrow$ $9f(x)=\alpha f(x)+\alpha xf^{'}(x)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha xf^{'}(x)=f(x)(9-\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha x}$ Integrating both sides $\int \frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}dx=\int \frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}(\frac{1}{x})dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $lnf(x)=\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}lnx+c$ $\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=e^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}lnx} \cdot e^{c}$ $\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=x^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}} \cdot K{K=e^{c}}$ It is given that $f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through $(2,1)$ and $(-4,\beta)$ . So $f(x)=Kx^{2}$ type. $\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}=2⟹9-\alpha=2\alpha⟹3\alpha=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=3$ $f(x)=Kx^{2}$ passing through $(2,1)$ $f(2)=1$ $1=K(2)^{2}⟹K=\frac{1}{4}$ $f(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{2}$ $f(x)$ is also passing through $(-4,\beta),f(-4)=\beta$ $\beta=\frac{1}{4}(-4)^{2}=\frac{16}{4}=4$ then $\beta^{\alpha}=4^{3}=64$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $\int_{0}^{36}f(\frac{tx}{36})dt=4\alpha f(x)$

Let $\frac{tx}{36}=u \Rightarrow \frac{x}{36}dt=du$

$\int_{0}^{x}f(u)\frac{36}{x}du=4\alpha f(x)$

Integration is w.r.t $u$ , so treat $x$ as a constant

$\int_{0}^{x}f(u)du=\frac{4x}{36}\alpha f(x)=\frac{x}{9}\alpha f(x)$

Now, differentiate both sides w.r.t $x$ , use Leibniz theorem in LHS:

$1 \cdot f(x)=\frac{\alpha}{9}[1 \cdot f(x)+xf^{'}(x)]$

$\Rightarrow$ $9f(x)=\alpha f(x)+\alpha xf^{'}(x)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha xf^{'}(x)=f(x)(9-\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha x}$

Integrating both sides

$\int \frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}dx=\int \frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}(\frac{1}{x})dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $lnf(x)=\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}lnx+c$

$\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=e^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}lnx} \cdot e^{c}$

$\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=x^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}} \cdot K{K=e^{c}}$

It is given that $f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through $(2,1)$ and $(-4,\beta)$ .

So $f(x)=Kx^{2}$ type.

$\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}=2⟹9-\alpha=2\alpha⟹3\alpha=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=3$

$f(x)=Kx^{2}$ passing through $(2,1)$

$f(2)=1$

$1=K(2)^{2}⟹K=\frac{1}{4}$

$f(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{2}$

$f(x)$ is also passing through $(-4,\beta),f(-4)=\beta$

$\beta=\frac{1}{4}(-4)^{2}=\frac{16}{4}=4$

then $\beta^{\alpha}=4^{3}=64$

questions.question_text: If $\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(1-2x+4x^{2})dx=atan^{-1}(2)-blog_{e}(5)$ , where $a,b \in N$ , then $(2a+b)$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.question_html: If $\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(1-2x+4x^{2})dx=atan^{-1}(2)-blog_{e}(5)$ , where $a,b \in N$ , then $(2a+b)$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: We are given $\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(1-2x+4x^{2})dx=atan^{-1}(2)-bln(5),a,b \in ℕ$ Step 1: Simplify the integrand $1-2x+4x^{2}=4x^{2}-2x+1>0∀x \in [0,1]$ For positive arguments, $cot^{-1}(u)=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{u})$ so $\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx=4\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{4x^{2}-2x+1})dx$ Using the identity $tan^{-1}(1/u)=\frac{\pi}{2}-tan^{-1}(u)$ (for $u>0$ ): $=4[\frac{\pi}{2}-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx]$ Step 2: Evaluate the remaining integral Using integration by parts and standard integrals of rational functions, one obtains: $\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx=tan^{-1}(3)-\frac{1}{4}ln5$ Substitute back: $\begin{aligned} I & =4[\frac{\pi}{2}-tan^{-1}(3)+\frac{1}{4}ln5] \\ & =4tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{3})+ln5 \end{aligned}$ Using the identity: $tan^{-1}(2)=2tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{3})$ we get: $I=4tan^{-1}(2)-ln5$ Step 3: Identify $a$ and $b$ Comparing with $atan^{-1}(2)-bln(5)$ we have: $a=4,b=1$ Final Answer $2a+b=2(4)+1=9$
questions.explanation_html:
We are given

$\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(1-2x+4x^{2})dx=atan^{-1}(2)-bln(5),a,b \in ℕ$

Step 1: Simplify the integrand

$1-2x+4x^{2}=4x^{2}-2x+1>0∀x \in [0,1]$

For positive arguments,

$cot^{-1}(u)=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{u})$

so

$\int_{0}^{1}4cot^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx=4\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{4x^{2}-2x+1})dx$

Using the identity $tan^{-1}(1/u)=\frac{\pi}{2}-tan^{-1}(u)$ (for $u>0$ ):

$=4[\frac{\pi}{2}-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx]$

Step 2: Evaluate the remaining integral

Using integration by parts and standard integrals of rational functions, one obtains:

$\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(4x^{2}-2x+1)dx=tan^{-1}(3)-\frac{1}{4}ln5$

Substitute back:

$\begin{aligned} I & =4[\frac{\pi}{2}-tan^{-1}(3)+\frac{1}{4}ln5] \\ & =4tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{3})+ln5 \end{aligned}$

Using the identity:

$tan^{-1}(2)=2tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{3})$

we get:

$I=4tan^{-1}(2)-ln5$

Step 3: Identify $a$ and $b$

Comparing with

$atan^{-1}(2)-bln(5)$

we have:

$a=4,b=1$

Final Answer

$2a+b=2(4)+1=9$

questions.question_html: Let $f(x)=⎧⎩⎨\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{3}, & x \le \pi/2 \\ \frac{b(1-sinx)}{(\pi-2x)^{2}}, & x>\pi/2 \end{aligned}$ . If $f$ is continuous at $x=\pi/2$ , then the value of $\int_{0}^{3b-6}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{𝝅}{2}$ where $f(x)=⎧⎩⎨\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{3} & ;x⩽\frac{\pi}{2} \\ \frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}} & ;x>\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}\cdot s(i)$ . We observe the LHL from equation $(i)$ : $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{\pi}{2})^{-}}{lim}f(x)=f(\frac{\pi}{2})=\frac{1}{3}\dots\dots(ii)$ We must have the RHL from equation (i) to be $\frac{1}{3}$ for the function $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=\frac{𝝅}{2}$ : $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}f(x)=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow \underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}}=\frac{1}{3}\dots\dots(iii)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}$ format $\le ftarrow$ Apply L'hôpital's rule $\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{bcosx}{4(𝝅-2x)}=\frac{0}{0}$ format ค Apply L'hôpital's rule once more $\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{\pi}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{bsinx}{8}=\frac{b}{8}\dots\dots(iv)$ We can mathematically demonstrate conditional continuity of $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ from equation (iii) and (iv) : $\frac{b}{8}=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow b=\frac{8}{3}\dots\dots(v)$ Now, I = $\int_{0}^{3b-6}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$ $=\int_{0}^{(3)(\frac{8}{3})-6}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$ $=\int_{0}^{2}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$ $=\int_{0}^{2}|(x+3)(x-1)|dx$ $⎧⎩⎨⎪⎪\begin{aligned} (x+3)(x-1)⩾0;x \in (-\infty,-3] \\ (x+3)(x-1)⩽0;x \in [-3,1] \\ (x+3)(x-1)⩾0;x \in [1,\infty) \end{aligned}$ $=\int_{0}^{1}(x+3)(1-x)dx$ $+\int_{1}^{2}(x+3)(x-1)dx$ $=\int_{0}^{1}(3-2x-x^{2})dx$ $+\int_{1}^{2}(x^{2}+2x-3)dx$ $\begin{aligned} & =[3x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}]_{0}^{1}+[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}-3x]_{1}^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =(3-1-\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{8}{3}+4-6)-(\frac{1}{3}+1-3) \end{aligned}$ = 4
questions.explanation_html:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{𝝅}{2}$ where

$f(x)=⎧⎩⎨\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{3} & ;x⩽\frac{\pi}{2} \\ \frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}} & ;x>\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}\cdot s(i)$ .

We observe the LHL from equation $(i)$ :

$\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{\pi}{2})^{-}}{lim}f(x)=f(\frac{\pi}{2})=\frac{1}{3}\dots\dots(ii)$

We must have the RHL from equation (i) to be $\frac{1}{3}$ for the function $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=\frac{𝝅}{2}$ :

$\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}f(x)=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow \underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}}=\frac{1}{3}\dots\dots(iii)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{b(1-sinx)}{(𝝅-2x)^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}$ format $\le ftarrow$ Apply L'hôpital's rule

$\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{𝝅}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{bcosx}{4(𝝅-2x)}=\frac{0}{0}$ format ค Apply L'hôpital's rule once more

$\Rightarrow$ $\underset{x \rightarrow (\frac{\pi}{2})^{+}}{lim}\frac{bsinx}{8}=\frac{b}{8}\dots\dots(iv)$

We can mathematically demonstrate conditional continuity of $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ from equation (iii) and (iv) :

$\frac{b}{8}=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow b=\frac{8}{3}\dots\dots(v)$

Now, I = $\int_{0}^{3b-6}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$

$=\int_{0}^{(3)(\frac{8}{3})-6}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$

$=\int_{0}^{2}|x^{2}+2x-3|dx$

$=\int_{0}^{2}|(x+3)(x-1)|dx$

$⎧⎩⎨⎪⎪\begin{aligned} (x+3)(x-1)⩾0;x \in (-\infty,-3] \\ (x+3)(x-1)⩽0;x \in [-3,1] \\ (x+3)(x-1)⩾0;x \in [1,\infty) \end{aligned}$

$=\int_{0}^{1}(x+3)(1-x)dx$ $+\int_{1}^{2}(x+3)(x-1)dx$

$=\int_{0}^{1}(3-2x-x^{2})dx$ $+\int_{1}^{2}(x^{2}+2x-3)dx$

$\begin{aligned} & =[3x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}]_{0}^{1}+[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}-3x]_{1}^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =(3-1-\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{8}{3}+4-6)-(\frac{1}{3}+1-3) \end{aligned}$

= 4

questions.question_text: The integral $\int_{0}^{1}cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})dx$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: The integral $\int_{0}^{1}cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})dx$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int_{0}^{1}cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})dx$ We will use the standard identity $cot^{-1}t=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{t})\text{for}t>0$ Since $1+x+x^{2}>0$ on $[0,1]$ , we can write $I=\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}})dx$ Now use the formula $tan^{-1}a-tan^{-1}b=tan^{-1}(\frac{a-b}{1+ab})$ We try to express $\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}}$ in a suitable form. Observe that $tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x=tan^{-1}(\frac{(x+1)-x}{1+x(x+1)})=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}})$ Hence, $cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})=tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x$ So, $I=\int_{0}^{1}[tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x]dx$ Therefore, $I=\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(x+1)dx-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx$ In the first integral, put $u=x+1$ . Then when $x=0$ , $u=1$ , and when $x=1$ , $u=2$ . So $\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(x+1)dx=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}udu$ Thus, $I=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}udu-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}xdx-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx$ Now use $\int tan^{-1}xdx=xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})$ So, $\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}xdx=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{1}^{2}$ and $\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{0}^{1}$ Hence, $I=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{1}^{2}-[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{0}^{1}$ This becomes $I=(2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5)-(tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}log2)-(tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}log2)$ since at $x=0$ , the value is $0$ . Now $tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , so $I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5-2(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}log2)$ $I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5-\frac{\pi}{2}+log2$ Now combine the logarithms: $log2-\frac{1}{2}log5=\frac{1}{2}log4-\frac{1}{2}log5=\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{4}{5})=-\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{5}{4})$ Therefore, $I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{5}{4})-\frac{\pi}{2}$ So the correct answer is $2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log_{e}(\frac{5}{4})-\frac{\pi}{2}$ Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option D}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$I=\int_{0}^{1}cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})dx$

We will use the standard identity

$cot^{-1}t=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{t})\text{for}t>0$

Since $1+x+x^{2}>0$ on $[0,1]$ , we can write

$I=\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}})dx$

Now use the formula

$tan^{-1}a-tan^{-1}b=tan^{-1}(\frac{a-b}{1+ab})$

We try to express

$\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}}$

in a suitable form. Observe that

$tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x=tan^{-1}(\frac{(x+1)-x}{1+x(x+1)})=tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{1+x+x^{2}})$

Hence,

$cot^{-1}(1+x+x^{2})=tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x$

So,

$I=\int_{0}^{1}[tan^{-1}(x+1)-tan^{-1}x]dx$

Therefore,

$I=\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(x+1)dx-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx$

In the first integral, put $u=x+1$ . Then when $x=0$ , $u=1$ , and when $x=1$ , $u=2$ . So

$\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}(x+1)dx=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}udu$

Thus,

$I=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}udu-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx=\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}xdx-\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx$

Now use

$\int tan^{-1}xdx=xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})$

So,

$\int_{1}^{2}tan^{-1}xdx=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{1}^{2}$

and

$\int_{0}^{1}tan^{-1}xdx=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{0}^{1}$

Hence,

$I=[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{1}^{2}-[xtan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})]_{0}^{1}$

This becomes

$I=(2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5)-(tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}log2)-(tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}log2)$

since at $x=0$ , the value is $0$ .

Now $tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , so

$I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5-2(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}log2)$

$I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log5-\frac{\pi}{2}+log2$

Now combine the logarithms:

$log2-\frac{1}{2}log5=\frac{1}{2}log4-\frac{1}{2}log5=\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{4}{5})=-\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{5}{4})$

Therefore,

$I=2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log(\frac{5}{4})-\frac{\pi}{2}$

So the correct answer is

$2tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}log_{e}(\frac{5}{4})-\frac{\pi}{2}$

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$

questions.question_text: Let $f$ be a differentiable function satisfying $f(x)=1-2x+\int_{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$ , $x \in ℝ$ and let $g(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$ , $x \in ℝ$ . If $p$ and $q$ are respectively the points of local minima and local maxima of $g$ , then the value of $|p+q|$ is equal to ________.
questions.question_html:
Let $f$ be a differentiable function satisfying $f(x)=1-2x+\int_{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$ , $x \in ℝ$ and let

$g(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$ , $x \in ℝ$ .

If $p$ and $q$ are respectively the points of local minima and local maxima of $g$ , then the value of $|p+q|$ is equal to ________.
questions.explanation_text: The given equation is: $f(x)=1-2x+\int_{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$ Since $e^{(x-t)}=e^{x} \cdot e^{-t}$ , we can move $e^{x}$ outside the integral because it is constant relative to $t$ $f(x)=1-2x+e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt$ Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule and the product rule: $f^{'}(x)=-2+[e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt+e^{x}(e^{-x}f(x))]$ Now, we use substitution from our original equation. Notice that $e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt=f(x)-(1-2x)$ . Substituting this back into the derivative expression: $f^{'}(x)=-2+[f(x)-1+2x]+f(x)$ $\Rightarrow$ $f^{'}(x)=2f(x)+2x-3$ Combine the terms to get the linear differential equatio in the form of $\frac{df(x)}{dx}+P(x)f(x)=Q(x)$ $\frac{df(x)}{dx}-2f(x)=2x-3$ Solve for $f(x)$ Integrating Factor (IF): $e^{\int -2dx}=e^{-2x}$ General Solution: $f(x) \cdot e^{-2x}=\int (2x-3)e^{-2x}dx$ By integrating the right side (Integration by Parts), we get $f(x)=1-x+Ce^{2x}$ . Using $f(0)=1$ (from the original equation), we find $C=0$ . Result: $f(x)=1-x$ . Find the Extrema of $g(x)$ $g(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$ Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule $g^{'}(x)=(f(x)+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17}$ Substitute $f(x)=1-x$ : $\begin{aligned} g^{'}(x)=(1-x+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \\ g^{'}(x)=(3-x)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \end{aligned}$ Critical points: $x=3,4,-12$ . Plot on number line to find local maxima and minima. Local Minima ( $p$ ): At $x=-12,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from negative to positive. Thus, $p=-12$ . Local Maxima ( $q$ ): At $x=3,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from positive to negative. Thus, $q=3$ . $x=4$ : No sign change occurs (even power 6), so it is not a local extremum. Final Answer $|p+q|=|-12+3|=|-9|=9$ The value of $|p+q|$ is 9 .
questions.explanation_html:
The given equation is:

$f(x)=1-2x+\int_{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$

Since $e^{(x-t)}=e^{x} \cdot e^{-t}$ , we can move $e^{x}$ outside the integral because it is constant relative to $t$

$f(x)=1-2x+e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule and the product rule:

$f^{'}(x)=-2+[e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt+e^{x}(e^{-x}f(x))]$

Now, we use substitution from our original equation. Notice that $e^{x}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt=f(x)-(1-2x)$ . Substituting this back into the derivative expression:

$f^{'}(x)=-2+[f(x)-1+2x]+f(x)$

$\Rightarrow$ $f^{'}(x)=2f(x)+2x-3$

Combine the terms to get the linear differential equatio in the form of $\frac{df(x)}{dx}+P(x)f(x)=Q(x)$

$\frac{df(x)}{dx}-2f(x)=2x-3$

Solve for $f(x)$

Integrating Factor (IF): $e^{\int -2dx}=e^{-2x}$

General Solution: $f(x) \cdot e^{-2x}=\int (2x-3)e^{-2x}dx$

By integrating the right side (Integration by Parts), we get $f(x)=1-x+Ce^{2x}$ .

Using $f(0)=1$ (from the original equation), we find $C=0$ .

Result: $f(x)=1-x$ .

Find the Extrema of $g(x)$

$g(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule

$g^{'}(x)=(f(x)+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17}$

Substitute $f(x)=1-x$ :

$\begin{aligned} g^{'}(x)=(1-x+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \\ g^{'}(x)=(3-x)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \end{aligned}$

Critical points: $x=3,4,-12$ .

Plot on number line to find local maxima and minima.

Local Minima ( $p$ ): At $x=-12,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from negative to positive. Thus, $p=-12$ .

Local Maxima ( $q$ ): At $x=3,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from positive to negative. Thus, $q=3$ .

$x=4$ : No sign change occurs (even power 6), so it is not a local extremum.

Final Answer

$|p+q|=|-12+3|=|-9|=9$

The value of $|p+q|$ is 9 .

questions.question_html: The number of elements in the set $S={x:x \in [0,100]$ and $\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}sin(x-t)dt=x^{2}}$ is $____$
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{x}t^{2}sin(x-t)dt=x^{2} \\ & \text{use property}\int_{0}^{a}f(t)dt=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-t)dt \\ & \int_{0}^{x}(x-t)^{2}sin(x-(x-t))dt=\int_{0}^{x}(x-t)^{2}sintdt=x^{2} \\ & \int_{0}^{x}(x^{2}-2xt+t^{2})sintdt=x^{2} \\ & x^{2}\int_{0}^{x}sintdt-2x\int_{0}^{x}tsintdt+\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}sintdt=x^{2} \end{aligned}$ differentiating with respect to $x$ (Leibniz rule): $\begin{aligned} & 2x\int_{0}^{x}sintdt+x^{2}sinx-2\int_{0}^{x}tsintdt-2x(xsinx)+x^{2}sinx=2x \\ & 2x\int_{0}^{x}sintdt-2\int_{0}^{x}tsintdt=2x \end{aligned}$ differentiating again: $\begin{aligned} & 2\int_{0}^{x}sintdt+2xsinx-2xsinx=2 \\ & 2[-cost]_{0}^{x}=2 \\ & -(cosx-cos0)=1 \\ & -cosx+1=1 \Rightarrow cosx=0 \end{aligned}$ finding number of elements in $S={x:x \in [0,100]$ and $cosx=0}$ $\begin{aligned} & x=(2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2} \\ & 0 \le (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2} \le 100 \Rightarrow 0 \le 2n+1 \le \frac{200}{\pi} \approx 63.66 \\ & 2n \le 62.66 \Rightarrow n \le 31.33 \end{aligned}$ for $n \in {0,1,2,\dots,31}$ , there are 32 values. the number of elements in set $S$ is 32 .

$\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{x}t^{2}sin(x-t)dt=x^{2} \\ & \text{use property}\int_{0}^{a}f(t)dt=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-t)dt \\ & \int_{0}^{x}(x-t)^{2}sin(x-(x-t))dt=\int_{0}^{x}(x-t)^{2}sintdt=x^{2} \\ & \int_{0}^{x}(x^{2}-2xt+t^{2})sintdt=x^{2} \\ & x^{2}\int_{0}^{x}sintdt-2x\int_{0}^{x}tsintdt+\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}sintdt=x^{2} \end{aligned}$

differentiating with respect to $x$ (Leibniz rule):

for $n \in {0,1,2,\dots,31}$ , there are 32 values.

the number of elements in set $S$ is 32 .

questions.explanation_text: Let, $I=\int_{0}^{\pi}|sin3x+sin2x+sinx|dx$ We know, $sin3x+sinx=2sin2xcosx$ $\therefore$ $sin3x+sin2x+sinx=2sin2xcosx+sin2x=sin2x(2cosx+1)$ $I=\int_{0}^{\pi}|sin2x(2cosx+1)|dx$ Critical points : $∀x \in [0,\pi]$ $sin2x=0 \Rightarrow x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi$ $\Rightarrow$ $2cosx+1=0 \Rightarrow cosx=-\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ $\begin{aligned} 2cosx+1>0 & ∀x \in [0,2\pi/3) \\ 2cosx+1 \le 0 & ∀x \in [2\pi/3,\pi] \end{aligned}$ Interval sign of sin 2x sign of 2 cos x + 1 sign of (sin 2x)(2 cos x + 1) (0, π/2) + + + (π/2, 2π/3) − + − (2π/3, π) − − + $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx-\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx+\int_{2\pi/3}^{\pi}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx$ Using, $sin2x=2sinxcosx$ $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx-\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx+\int_{2\pi/3}^{\pi}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx$ Let $t=cosx,sinxdx=-dt$ , limits get change $I=\int_{1}^{0}-2(2t^{2}+t)dt+\int_{0}^{-1/2}2(2t^{2}+t)dt-\int_{-1/2}^{-1}2(2t^{2}+t)dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=2\int_{0}^{1}(2t^{2}+t)dt-2\int_{-1/2}^{0}(2t^{2}+t)dt+2\int_{-1}^{-1/2}(2t^{2}+t)dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=2[(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{-1}^{-1/2}-(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{-1/2}^{0}+(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{0}^{1}]$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Ist part}=[\frac{2}{3}(-1/2)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1/2)^{2}-{\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{2}}]=[-1/12+1/8+2/3-1/2]=\frac{5}{24} \\ & \text{IInd part}=[\frac{2}{3}(0)+0-{\frac{2}{3}(-1/2)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1/2)^{2}}]=[1/12-1/8]=-\frac{1}{24} \\ & \text{IIIrd part}=[\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-{0+0}]=\frac{7}{6}=\frac{28}{24} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=2[\frac{5}{24}-(-1/24)+\frac{28}{24}]=2 \times \frac{34}{24}=\frac{17}{6}$ $\Rightarrow 6I=17$

Let, $I=\int_{0}^{\pi}|sin3x+sin2x+sinx|dx$

We know, $sin3x+sinx=2sin2xcosx$

$\therefore$ $sin3x+sin2x+sinx=2sin2xcosx+sin2x=sin2x(2cosx+1)$

$I=\int_{0}^{\pi}|sin2x(2cosx+1)|dx$

Critical points : $∀x \in [0,\pi]$

$sin2x=0 \Rightarrow x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi$

$\Rightarrow$ $2cosx+1=0 \Rightarrow cosx=-\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x=\frac{2\pi}{3}$

$\begin{aligned} 2cosx+1>0 & ∀x \in [0,2\pi/3) \\ 2cosx+1 \le 0 & ∀x \in [2\pi/3,\pi] \end{aligned}$

Interval sign of sin 2x sign of 2 cos x + 1 sign of (sin 2x)(2 cos x + 1)
(0, π/2) + + +
(π/2, 2π/3) − + −
(2π/3, π) − − +

$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx-\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx+\int_{2\pi/3}^{\pi}sin2x(2cosx+1)dx$

Using, $sin2x=2sinxcosx$

$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx-\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx+\int_{2\pi/3}^{\pi}2sinx(2cos^{2}x+cosx)dx$

Let $t=cosx,sinxdx=-dt$ , limits get change

$I=\int_{1}^{0}-2(2t^{2}+t)dt+\int_{0}^{-1/2}2(2t^{2}+t)dt-\int_{-1/2}^{-1}2(2t^{2}+t)dt$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=2\int_{0}^{1}(2t^{2}+t)dt-2\int_{-1/2}^{0}(2t^{2}+t)dt+2\int_{-1}^{-1/2}(2t^{2}+t)dt$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=2[(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{-1}^{-1/2}-(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{-1/2}^{0}+(\frac{2t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{2}}{2})_{0}^{1}]$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Ist part}=[\frac{2}{3}(-1/2)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1/2)^{2}-{\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{2}}]=[-1/12+1/8+2/3-1/2]=\frac{5}{24} \\ & \text{IInd part}=[\frac{2}{3}(0)+0-{\frac{2}{3}(-1/2)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(-1/2)^{2}}]=[1/12-1/8]=-\frac{1}{24} \\ & \text{IIIrd part}=[\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-{0+0}]=\frac{7}{6}=\frac{28}{24} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=2[\frac{5}{24}-(-1/24)+\frac{28}{24}]=2 \times \frac{34}{24}=\frac{17}{6}$

$\Rightarrow 6I=17$

questions.question_text: Let $A=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$ be a singular matrix. Let $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(t^{2}+2t+3)dt,x \in [1,\alpha]$ . If M and m are respectively the maximum and the minimum values of $f$ in $[1,\alpha]$ , then $3(M-m)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $A=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$ be a singular matrix. Let $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(t^{2}+2t+3)dt,x \in [1,\alpha]$ . If M and m are respectively the maximum and the minimum values of $f$ in $[1,\alpha]$ , then $3(M-m)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Since $A$ is a singular matrix, its determinant must be zero. We have $A=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$ So, $|A|=0$ Now let us calculate the determinant by expanding along the first row: $|A|=1|\begin{aligned} 1 & \alpha \\ 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned} 2 & \alpha \\ 0 & -1 \end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=1[(1)(-1)-(\alpha)(1)]-3[(2)(-1)-(\alpha)(0)]-1[(2)(1)-(1)(0)]$ $=(-1-\alpha)-3(-2)-2$ $=-1-\alpha+6-2$ $=3-\alpha$ Since $|A|=0$ , $3-\alpha=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=3$ Now, $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(t^{2}+2t+3)dt$ Integrating, $f(x)=[\frac{t^{3}}{3}+t^{2}+3t]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$ We need maximum and minimum values of $f(x)$ in $[1,\alpha]=[1,3]$ . Now check whether $f(x)$ is increasing or decreasing. $f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3$ $f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3=(x+1)^{2}+2>0\text{for all}x$ So $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[1,3]$ . Hence, minimum value at $x=1$ maximum value at $x=3$ Now, $m=f(1)=\frac{1}{3}+1+3=\frac{13}{3}$ and $M=f(3)=\frac{27}{3}+9+9=9+9+9=27$ Therefore, $M-m=27-\frac{13}{3}=\frac{81-13}{3}=\frac{68}{3}$ So, $3(M-m)=3 \cdot \frac{68}{3}=68$ Hence the correct answer is: $68$ So, the correct option is $\text{Option B}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Since $A$ is a singular matrix, its determinant must be zero.

We have

$A=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$

So,

$|A|=0$

Now let us calculate the determinant by expanding along the first row:

$|A|=1|\begin{aligned} 1 & \alpha \\ 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned} 2 & \alpha \\ 0 & -1 \end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=1[(1)(-1)-(\alpha)(1)]-3[(2)(-1)-(\alpha)(0)]-1[(2)(1)-(1)(0)]$

$=(-1-\alpha)-3(-2)-2$

$=-1-\alpha+6-2$

$=3-\alpha$

Since $|A|=0$ ,

$3-\alpha=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=3$

Now,

$f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}(t^{2}+2t+3)dt$

Integrating,

$f(x)=[\frac{t^{3}}{3}+t^{2}+3t]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$

We need maximum and minimum values of $f(x)$ in $[1,\alpha]=[1,3]$ .

Now check whether $f(x)$ is increasing or decreasing.

$f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3$

$f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3=(x+1)^{2}+2>0\text{for all}x$

So $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[1,3]$ .

Hence,

  • minimum value at $x=1$

  • maximum value at $x=3$

Now,

$m=f(1)=\frac{1}{3}+1+3=\frac{13}{3}$

and

$M=f(3)=\frac{27}{3}+9+9=9+9+9=27$

Therefore,

$M-m=27-\frac{13}{3}=\frac{81-13}{3}=\frac{68}{3}$

So,

$3(M-m)=3 \cdot \frac{68}{3}=68$

Hence the correct answer is:

$68$

So, the correct option is $\text{Option B}$ .

questions.question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{log_{e}(x)}{x^{2}+4}dx$ is:
questions.question_html: The value of the integral $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{log_{e}(x)}{x^{2}+4}dx$ is:
questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnx}{x^{2}+4}dx$ We will use a standard substitution, as done in NCERT-type definite integral problems. Take $x=2t$ Then $dx=2dt$ and when $x=0,t=0$ , and when $x \rightarrow \infty,t \rightarrow \infty$ . So, $I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{(2t)^{2}+4} \cdot 2dt$ Simplify the denominator: $(2t)^{2}+4=4t^{2}+4=4(1+t^{2})$ Hence, $I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{4(1+t^{2})} \cdot 2dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{1+t^{2}}dt$ Now use $ln(2t)=ln2+lnt$ So, $I=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln2}{1+t^{2}}dt+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$ That is, $I=\frac{ln2}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$ Now, $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}=[tan^{-1}t]_{0}^{\infty}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ Also, let $J=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$ Using the substitution $t=\frac{1}{u}$ , we get $dt=-\frac{1}{u^{2}}du$ Then $J=\int_{\infty}^{0}\frac{ln(1/u)}{1+1/u^{2}}(-\frac{1}{u^{2}})du$ This simplifies to $J=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{-lnu}{1+u^{2}}du=-J$ Therefore, $J=0$ So, $I=\frac{ln2}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi ln2}{4}$ Hence, the value of the integral is $\frac{\pi ln2}{4}$ So, the correct option is: $\text{Option B}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnx}{x^{2}+4}dx$

We will use a standard substitution, as done in NCERT-type definite integral problems.

Take

$x=2t$

Then

$dx=2dt$

and when $x=0,t=0$ , and when $x \rightarrow \infty,t \rightarrow \infty$ .

So,

$I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{(2t)^{2}+4} \cdot 2dt$

Simplify the denominator:

$(2t)^{2}+4=4t^{2}+4=4(1+t^{2})$

Hence,

$I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{4(1+t^{2})} \cdot 2dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln(2t)}{1+t^{2}}dt$

Now use

$ln(2t)=ln2+lnt$

So,

$I=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{ln2}{1+t^{2}}dt+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$

That is,

$I=\frac{ln2}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$

Now,

$\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}=[tan^{-1}t]_{0}^{\infty}=\frac{\pi}{2}$

Also, let

$J=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{lnt}{1+t^{2}}dt$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{1}{u}$ , we get

$dt=-\frac{1}{u^{2}}du$

Then

$J=\int_{\infty}^{0}\frac{ln(1/u)}{1+1/u^{2}}(-\frac{1}{u^{2}})du$

This simplifies to

$J=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{-lnu}{1+u^{2}}du=-J$

Therefore,

$J=0$

So,

$I=\frac{ln2}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi ln2}{4}$

Hence, the value of the integral is

$\frac{\pi ln2}{4}$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option B}$

questions.question_text: Let $f$ be a real polynomial of degree $n$ such that $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ , for all $x \in ℝ$ . If $f(0)=0$ , then $36(f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx)$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Let $f$ be a real polynomial of degree $n$ such that $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ , for all $x \in ℝ$ . If $f(0)=0$ , then $36(f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Let the degree of the real polynomial $f$ be $n$ . Since $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ for all $x$ , we compare degrees: $\begin{aligned} & deg(f)=deg(f^{'})+deg(f^{''}) \\ & n=(n-1)+(n-2)=2n-3 \\ & \Rightarrow n=3 \end{aligned}$ So $f$ must be a cubic polynomial. Write $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d \end{aligned}$ Given $f(0)=0$ , we get $d=0$ . Hence $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx \end{aligned}$ Now find derivatives: $\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c \\ & f^{''}(x)=6ax+2b \end{aligned}$ Use the given condition $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ : $\begin{aligned} & (ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx)=(3ax^{2}+2bx+c)(6ax+2b) \end{aligned}$ Now compare coefficients of like powers of $x$ . For $x^{3}$ : $\begin{aligned} & a=18a^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{18}(\text{since}a \ne 0\text{for a cubic}) \end{aligned}$ For $x^{2}$ : $\begin{aligned} & b=6ab+12ab \\ & b=18ab \end{aligned}$ With $a=\frac{1}{18}$ , this becomes $b=b$ , so it gives no new condition on $b$ . For $x$ : $\begin{aligned} & c=4b^{2}+6ac \\ & c=4b^{2}+\frac{c}{3}( \because 6a=\frac{1}{3}) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2c}{3}=4b^{2} \Rightarrow c=6b^{2} \end{aligned}$ For the constant term: $\begin{aligned} & 0=2bc \Rightarrow bc=0 \end{aligned}$ But $c=6b^{2}$ , so $bc=b(6b^{2})=6b^{3}=0 \Rightarrow b=0$ , and then $c=0$ . So the polynomial is $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\frac{1}{18}x^{3} \end{aligned}$ Now compute the required value: $\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{6}x^{2} \Rightarrow f^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{6} \cdot 4=\frac{2}{3} \\ & f^{''}(x)=\frac{1}{3}x \Rightarrow f^{''}(2)=\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2=\frac{2}{3} \\ & \int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{18}x^{3}dx=\frac{1}{18}[\frac{x^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{18} \cdot \frac{16}{4}=\frac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$ Add them: $\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx \\ & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{14}{9} \end{aligned}$ Finally, $\begin{aligned} & 36(f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx)=36 \cdot \frac{14}{9}=56 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the degree of the real polynomial $f$ be $n$ .

Since $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ for all $x$ , we compare degrees:

$\begin{aligned} & deg(f)=deg(f^{'})+deg(f^{''}) \\ & n=(n-1)+(n-2)=2n-3 \\ & \Rightarrow n=3 \end{aligned}$

So $f$ must be a cubic polynomial. Write

$\begin{aligned} & f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d \end{aligned}$

Given $f(0)=0$ , we get $d=0$ . Hence

$\begin{aligned} & f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx \end{aligned}$

Now find derivatives:

$\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c \\ & f^{''}(x)=6ax+2b \end{aligned}$

Use the given condition $f(x)=f^{'}(x)f^{''}(x)$ :

$\begin{aligned} & (ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx)=(3ax^{2}+2bx+c)(6ax+2b) \end{aligned}$

Now compare coefficients of like powers of $x$ .

For $x^{3}$ :

$\begin{aligned} & a=18a^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{18}(\text{since}a \ne 0\text{for a cubic}) \end{aligned}$

For $x^{2}$ :

$\begin{aligned} & b=6ab+12ab \\ & b=18ab \end{aligned}$

With $a=\frac{1}{18}$ , this becomes $b=b$ , so it gives no new condition on $b$ .

For $x$ :

$\begin{aligned} & c=4b^{2}+6ac \\ & c=4b^{2}+\frac{c}{3}( \because 6a=\frac{1}{3}) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2c}{3}=4b^{2} \Rightarrow c=6b^{2} \end{aligned}$

For the constant term:

$\begin{aligned} & 0=2bc \Rightarrow bc=0 \end{aligned}$

But $c=6b^{2}$ , so $bc=b(6b^{2})=6b^{3}=0 \Rightarrow b=0$ , and then $c=0$ .

So the polynomial is

$\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\frac{1}{18}x^{3} \end{aligned}$

Now compute the required value:

$\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{6}x^{2} \Rightarrow f^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{6} \cdot 4=\frac{2}{3} \\ & f^{''}(x)=\frac{1}{3}x \Rightarrow f^{''}(2)=\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2=\frac{2}{3} \\ & \int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{18}x^{3}dx=\frac{1}{18}[\frac{x^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{18} \cdot \frac{16}{4}=\frac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$

Add them:

$\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx \\ & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{14}{9} \end{aligned}$

Finally,

$\begin{aligned} & 36(f^{'}(2)+f^{''}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx)=36 \cdot \frac{14}{9}=56 \end{aligned}$

Let [.] denote the greatest integer function. Then

$\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\frac{12(3+[x])}{3+[sinx]+[cosx]})dx$
is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\frac{12(3+[x])}{3+[sinx]+[cosx]})dx$ Breakdown the Interval Since $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$ and $-\frac{\pi}{2} \approx -1.57$ , we break the integral at the integer points $x=-1,0,1$ . Interval [x] [sin x] [cos x] Integrand f (x) $[-\frac{\pi}{2},-1)$ −2 −1 0 $\frac{12(3-2)}{3-1+0}=\frac{12}{2}=6$ [−1, 0) −1 −1 0 $\frac{12(3-1)}{3-1+0}=\frac{24}{2}=12$ [0, 1) 0 0 0 $\frac{12(3+0)}{3+0+0}=\frac{36}{3}=12$ $[1,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ 1 0 0 $\frac{12(3+1)}{3+0+0}=\frac{48}{3}=16$ Notes on values : 1. For $x \in (0,1),0<cosx<1$ , so $[cosx]=0$ . (At $x=0,[cosx]=1$ , but a single point doesn't change the integral). 2. For $x \in [1,\frac{\pi}{2}),0<sinx<1$ , so $[sinx]=0$ . To find the total value, we integrate the constant values found above over their respective subintervals: $I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{-1}6dx+\int_{-1}^{1}12dx+\int_{1}^{\pi/2}16dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=6[x]_{-\pi/2}^{-1}+12[x]_{-1}^{1}+16[x]_{1}^{\pi/2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=6(-1-(-\frac{\pi}{2}))+12(1-(-1))+16(\frac{\pi}{2}-1)$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=-6+3\pi+24+8\pi-16I=11\pi+2$
questions.explanation_html:
$I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\frac{12(3+[x])}{3+[sinx]+[cosx]})dx$

Breakdown the Interval Since $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$ and $-\frac{\pi}{2} \approx -1.57$ , we break the integral at the integer points $x=-1,0,1$ .

Interval [x] [sin x] [cos x] Integrand f(x)
$[-\frac{\pi}{2},-1)$ −2 −1 0 $\frac{12(3-2)}{3-1+0}=\frac{12}{2}=6$
[−1, 0) −1 −1 0 $\frac{12(3-1)}{3-1+0}=\frac{24}{2}=12$
[0, 1) 0 0 0 $\frac{12(3+0)}{3+0+0}=\frac{36}{3}=12$
$[1,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ 1 0 0 $\frac{12(3+1)}{3+0+0}=\frac{48}{3}=16$

Notes on values :

  • 1. For $x \in (0,1),0<cosx<1$ , so $[cosx]=0$ . (At $x=0,[cosx]=1$ , but a single point doesn't change the integral).

    2. For $x \in [1,\frac{\pi}{2}),0<sinx<1$ , so $[sinx]=0$ .

To find the total value, we integrate the constant values found above over their respective subintervals:

$I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{-1}6dx+\int_{-1}^{1}12dx+\int_{1}^{\pi/2}16dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=6[x]_{-\pi/2}^{-1}+12[x]_{-1}^{1}+16[x]_{1}^{\pi/2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=6(-1-(-\frac{\pi}{2}))+12(1-(-1))+16(\frac{\pi}{2}-1)$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=-6+3\pi+24+8\pi-16I=11\pi+2$

questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & 6\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt=3xf(x)+x^{2}-4 \\ & \text{By using leibnz rule} \\ & \begin{aligned} & 6f(x)=3f(x)+3xf^{'}(x)+3x^{2} \\ & \frac{f(x)-xf^{'}(x)}{x^{2}}=1 \\ & \frac{d}{dx}(\frac{f(x)}{x})=-1f(x)=-x^{2}+kx \\ & 1=-1+k(\text{since}f(1)=1) \\ & f(x)=-x^{2}+2x \\ & f(2)-f(3)=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Let $J_{r}=\int_{0}^{r}x \cdot |sin\pi x|dx$ So we need to calculate $I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi J_{r}}$ So, $I=\sqrt{\pi}(J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3}+\cdot s+J_{20})$ Let $\pi x=t \Rightarrow \pi dx=dt$ $J_{r}=\int_{0}^{\pi r}\frac{t}{\pi}|sint|\frac{dt}{\pi}=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi r}t|sint|dt$ Period of $|sint|$ is $\pi$ , so break the interval $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\pi r}t|sint|=\int_{0}^{\pi}t|sint|dt+\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}t|sint|dt+\int_{2\pi}^{3\pi}t|sint|dt+\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt \\ & \text{Now} \\ & |sint|=sint\text{for Ist and II Quadrant} \\ & |sint|=-sint\text{for III and IV Quadrant} \end{aligned}$ $\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=\int_{0}^{\pi}tsintdt-\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}tsintdt+\int_{2\pi}^{3\pi}tsintdt-\int_{3\pi}^{4\pi}tsint\dots(-1)^{r-1}\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsintdt$ Solving $\int t \cdot sint$ using by parts $\int u \cdot vdx=u \cdot \int vdx-\int (u^{'}\int vdv)dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int t \cdot sint=(-tcost)-\int 1 \cdot (-cost)=-tcost+sint$ Substituting the limits $\Rightarrow$ $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\pi r}t \cdot |sint|dt=[-tcost+sint]_{0}^{\pi}-[-tcost+sint]_{\pi}^{2\pi}+[-tcost+sint]_{2\pi}^{3\pi}-[-tcost+sint]_{3\pi}^{4\pi}\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsint(-1)^{r-1}dt \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =[\pi+0-0]-[-2\pi+0-{\pi+0}]+[3\pi+0-{-2\pi}+0]-[-4\pi-{-3\pi+0}]+\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsint(-1)^{r-1}dt \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=[\pi+0]+[2\pi+\pi]+[3\pi+2\pi]+[4\pi+3\pi]\dots[r\pi+(r-1)\pi]$ $\begin{aligned} & =\pi+3\pi+5\pi+7\pi+\dots(2r-1)\pi \\ \\ & =\pi(1+3+5+7+\dots(2r-1)) \end{aligned}$ Sum of first $r$ odd numbers is $r^{2}$ $\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=\pi r^{2}$ $J_{r}=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\pi r^{2}=\frac{r^{2}}{\pi}$ so, $I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi \cdot J_{r}}=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi \cdot \frac{r^{2}}{\pi}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}r=1+2+3+\dots20$ $\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{20 \times 21}{2}=210$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $J_{r}=\int_{0}^{r}x \cdot |sin\pi x|dx$

So we need to calculate

$I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi J_{r}}$

So,

$I=\sqrt{\pi}(J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3}+\cdot s+J_{20})$

Let $\pi x=t \Rightarrow \pi dx=dt$

$J_{r}=\int_{0}^{\pi r}\frac{t}{\pi}|sint|\frac{dt}{\pi}=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi r}t|sint|dt$

Period of $|sint|$ is $\pi$ , so break the interval

$\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\pi r}t|sint|=\int_{0}^{\pi}t|sint|dt+\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}t|sint|dt+\int_{2\pi}^{3\pi}t|sint|dt+\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt \\ & \text{Now} \\ & |sint|=sint\text{for Ist and II Quadrant} \\ & |sint|=-sint\text{for III and IV Quadrant} \end{aligned}$

$\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=\int_{0}^{\pi}tsintdt-\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}tsintdt+\int_{2\pi}^{3\pi}tsintdt-\int_{3\pi}^{4\pi}tsint\dots(-1)^{r-1}\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsintdt$

Solving $\int t \cdot sint$ using by parts

$\int u \cdot vdx=u \cdot \int vdx-\int (u^{'}\int vdv)dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $\int t \cdot sint=(-tcost)-\int 1 \cdot (-cost)=-tcost+sint$

Substituting the limits

$\Rightarrow$ $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\pi r}t \cdot |sint|dt=[-tcost+sint]_{0}^{\pi}-[-tcost+sint]_{\pi}^{2\pi}+[-tcost+sint]_{2\pi}^{3\pi}-[-tcost+sint]_{3\pi}^{4\pi}\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsint(-1)^{r-1}dt \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =[\pi+0-0]-[-2\pi+0-{\pi+0}]+[3\pi+0-{-2\pi}+0]-[-4\pi-{-3\pi+0}]+\cdot s\int_{(r-1)\pi}^{r\pi}tsint(-1)^{r-1}dt \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=[\pi+0]+[2\pi+\pi]+[3\pi+2\pi]+[4\pi+3\pi]\dots[r\pi+(r-1)\pi]$

$\begin{aligned} & =\pi+3\pi+5\pi+7\pi+\dots(2r-1)\pi \\ \\ & =\pi(1+3+5+7+\dots(2r-1)) \end{aligned}$

Sum of first $r$ odd numbers is $r^{2}$

$\int_{0}^{r\pi}t|sint|dt=\pi r^{2}$

$J_{r}=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\pi r^{2}=\frac{r^{2}}{\pi}$

so,

$I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi \cdot J_{r}}=\sum_{r=1}^{20}\sqrt{\pi \cdot \frac{r^{2}}{\pi}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\sum_{r=1}^{20}r=1+2+3+\dots20$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{20 \times 21}{2}=210$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{64}X^{\frac{1}{3}}dx=\frac{3}{4} \cdot [X^{\frac{4}{3}}]_{0}^{64}=192& \\ & \int_{0}^{64}[X^{1/3}]dx=\int_{0}^{1}[X^{1/3}]dx+\int_{1}^{8}[X^{1/3}]dx+\int_{8}^{27}[X^{1/3}]dx\int_{27}^{64}[X^{1/3}]dx=156 \end{aligned}$ So $\alpha=192-156=36$ Now $E=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{36\pi}\frac{sin^{2}_{\theta}}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta=\frac{36}{\pi} \cdot 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta$ $\Rightarrow E=\frac{36}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta$ Let $J=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta\dots\dots\dots$ Applying King $J=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{cos^{2}\theta}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta\dots\dots\dots.$ . Now $2J=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{sin^{6}\theta+cos^{6}\theta}d\theta(add(1)&(2))=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{sec^{6}\theta}{tan^{6}\theta+1}d\theta$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Put}tan\theta=\lambda \\ & \begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{(1+\lambda^{2})^{2}}{\lambda^{4}-\lambda^{2}+1}d\lambda \\ & \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1+\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}}{\lambda^{2}-1+\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}}d\lambda=\pi \\ & \Rightarrow J=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ & E=\frac{36}{\pi} \cdot 2J=36 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Let the given integral be denoted by $I$ . We can split $I$ into two separate integrals: $I=\int_{-2}^{2}(|sinx|+[xsinx])dx=\int_{-2}^{2}|sinx|dx+\int_{-2}^{2}[xsinx]dx$ Let $I_{1}=\int_{-2}^{2}|sinx|dx$ and $I_{2}=\int_{-2}^{2}[xsinx]dx$ . Step 1: Evaluate $I_{1}$ Based on the property of definite integrals, if $f(x)$ is an even function (i.e., $f(-x)=f(x)$ ), then $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx=2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx$ . Since $|sin(-x)|=|-sinx|=|sinx|$ , the function is even. Thus, $I_{1}=2\int_{0}^{2}|sinx|dx$ In the interval $[0,2]$ , $2$ radians is less than $\pi( \approx 3.14)$ , so $sinx>0$ . Hence, $|sinx|=sinx$ . $I_{1}=2\int_{0}^{2}sinxdx$ $I_{1}=2[-cosx]_{0}^{2}=2(-cos2-(-cos0))$ $I_{1}=2(1-cos2)=2-2cos2$ Step 2: Evaluate $I_{2}$ Let $f(x)=xsinx$ . We check if it is even or odd: $f(-x)=(-x)sin(-x)=(-x)(-sinx)=xsinx=f(x)$ . Since $f(x)$ is an even function, $[xsinx]$ is also an even function. $I_{2}=2\int_{0}^{2}[xsinx]dx$ Now, let us analyze the behavior of $f(x)=xsinx$ in the interval $x \in [0,2]$ : When $x=0$ , $f(0)=0$ . When $x=2$ , $f(2)=2sin2$ . Notice that $\pi/2<2<2\pi/3$ , meaning $sin2$ is between $sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $sin(2\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$ . So, $1.732<2sin2<2$ . Hence, the maximum value of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ is between $1$ and $2$ . Let's verify if $f(x)$ is strictly increasing in $[0,2]$ . We differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$ : $f^{'}(x)=sinx+xcosx$ For $x \in (0,\pi/2]$ , both $sinx>0$ and $cosx \ge 0$ , so $f^{'}(x)>0$ . For $x \in (\pi/2,2]$ , $cosx<0$ . We can rewrite $f^{'}(x)$ as: $f^{'}(x)=cosx(tanx+x)$ Since $tanx$ is negative in the second quadrant and $2$ radians is smaller than $tan^{-1}(-2)$ , the expression $(tanx+x)$ evaluates to a negative value. Therefore, $cosx$ (negative) $\times$ $(tanx+x)$ (negative) will yield $f^{'}(x)>0$ . Since $f(x)$ strictly increases from $0$ to a value between $1$ and $2$ , there is exactly one real number $\alpha \in (0,2)$ at which $f(\alpha)=1$ . So, $\alpha sin\alpha=1$ For $x \in [0,\alpha)$ , the function values are $0 \le xsinx<1$ , which gives $[xsinx]=0$ . For $x \in [\alpha,2]$ , the function values are $1 \le xsinx<2$ , which gives $[xsinx]=1$ . Now, split the integral $I_{2}$ at $x=\alpha$ : $I_{2}=2(\int_{0}^{\alpha}0dx+\int_{\alpha}^{2}1dx)$ $I_{2}=2[x]_{\alpha}^{2}=2(2-\alpha)=4-2\alpha$ Step 3: Finding the value of $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})$ Combining $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ , we get the total integral: $I=I_{1}+I_{2}=(2-2cos2)+(4-2\alpha)=6-2cos2-2\alpha$ $I=2(3-cos2)-2\alpha$ According to the question, the total integral evaluates to: $I=2(3-cos2)+\beta$ Comparing our result with the given equation, we find: $\beta=-2\alpha$ Finally, substituting $\beta=-2\alpha$ into the expression $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})$ : $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=-2\alpha \cdot sin(\frac{-2\alpha}{2})$ $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=-2\alpha \cdot sin(-\alpha)=-2\alpha(-sin\alpha)$ $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=2(\alpha sin\alpha)$ From our earlier deduction in Step 2, we established that $\alpha sin\alpha=1$ . Therefore: $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=2(1)=2$ Option B is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_html:
Let the given integral be denoted by $I$ . We can split $I$ into two separate integrals:

$I=\int_{-2}^{2}(|sinx|+[xsinx])dx=\int_{-2}^{2}|sinx|dx+\int_{-2}^{2}[xsinx]dx$

Let $I_{1}=\int_{-2}^{2}|sinx|dx$ and $I_{2}=\int_{-2}^{2}[xsinx]dx$ .

Step 1: Evaluate $I_{1}$

Based on the property of definite integrals, if $f(x)$ is an even function (i.e., $f(-x)=f(x)$ ), then $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx=2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx$ .

Since $|sin(-x)|=|-sinx|=|sinx|$ , the function is even. Thus,

$I_{1}=2\int_{0}^{2}|sinx|dx$

In the interval $[0,2]$ , $2$ radians is less than $\pi( \approx 3.14)$ , so $sinx>0$ . Hence, $|sinx|=sinx$ .

$I_{1}=2\int_{0}^{2}sinxdx$

$I_{1}=2[-cosx]_{0}^{2}=2(-cos2-(-cos0))$

$I_{1}=2(1-cos2)=2-2cos2$

Step 2: Evaluate $I_{2}$

Let $f(x)=xsinx$ . We check if it is even or odd:

$f(-x)=(-x)sin(-x)=(-x)(-sinx)=xsinx=f(x)$ .

Since $f(x)$ is an even function, $[xsinx]$ is also an even function.

$I_{2}=2\int_{0}^{2}[xsinx]dx$

Now, let us analyze the behavior of $f(x)=xsinx$ in the interval $x \in [0,2]$ :

  • When $x=0$ , $f(0)=0$ .

  • When $x=2$ , $f(2)=2sin2$ .

Notice that $\pi/2<2<2\pi/3$ , meaning $sin2$ is between $sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $sin(2\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$ .

So, $1.732<2sin2<2$ . Hence, the maximum value of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ is between $1$ and $2$ .

Let's verify if $f(x)$ is strictly increasing in $[0,2]$ . We differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$ :

$f^{'}(x)=sinx+xcosx$

For $x \in (0,\pi/2]$ , both $sinx>0$ and $cosx \ge 0$ , so $f^{'}(x)>0$ .

For $x \in (\pi/2,2]$ , $cosx<0$ . We can rewrite $f^{'}(x)$ as:

$f^{'}(x)=cosx(tanx+x)$

Since $tanx$ is negative in the second quadrant and $2$ radians is smaller than $tan^{-1}(-2)$ , the expression $(tanx+x)$ evaluates to a negative value. Therefore, $cosx$ (negative) $\times$ $(tanx+x)$ (negative) will yield $f^{'}(x)>0$ .

Since $f(x)$ strictly increases from $0$ to a value between $1$ and $2$ , there is exactly one real number $\alpha \in (0,2)$ at which $f(\alpha)=1$ . So,

$\alpha sin\alpha=1$

For $x \in [0,\alpha)$ , the function values are $0 \le xsinx<1$ , which gives $[xsinx]=0$ .

For $x \in [\alpha,2]$ , the function values are $1 \le xsinx<2$ , which gives $[xsinx]=1$ .

Now, split the integral $I_{2}$ at $x=\alpha$ :

$I_{2}=2(\int_{0}^{\alpha}0dx+\int_{\alpha}^{2}1dx)$

$I_{2}=2[x]_{\alpha}^{2}=2(2-\alpha)=4-2\alpha$

Step 3: Finding the value of $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})$

Combining $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ , we get the total integral:

$I=I_{1}+I_{2}=(2-2cos2)+(4-2\alpha)=6-2cos2-2\alpha$

$I=2(3-cos2)-2\alpha$

According to the question, the total integral evaluates to:

$I=2(3-cos2)+\beta$

Comparing our result with the given equation, we find:

$\beta=-2\alpha$

Finally, substituting $\beta=-2\alpha$ into the expression $\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})$ :

$\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=-2\alpha \cdot sin(\frac{-2\alpha}{2})$

$\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=-2\alpha \cdot sin(-\alpha)=-2\alpha(-sin\alpha)$

$\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=2(\alpha sin\alpha)$

From our earlier deduction in Step 2, we established that $\alpha sin\alpha=1$ . Therefore:

$\beta sin(\frac{\beta}{2})=2(1)=2$

Option B is the correct answer.

questions.explanation_text: We are given the functional equation: $f(x^{2}+1)=x^{4}+5x^{2}+2$ Let $t=x^{2}+1$ . This implies that $x^{2}=t-1$ . Now, substitute this into the right side of the equation: $\begin{aligned} f(t)=(t-1)^{2}+5(t-1)+2 \\ f(t)=(t^{2}-2t+1)+5t-5+2 \\ f(t)=t^{2}+3t-2 \end{aligned}$ Replacing $t$ back with $x$ , the polynomial function is: $f(x)=x^{2}+3x-2$ Now, we calculate the definite integral from 0 to 3 : $\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{3}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{3}(x^{2}+3x-2)dx \\ [\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{3x^{2}}{2}-2x]_{0}^{3} \\ =(\frac{3^{3}}{3}+\frac{3(3^{2})}{2}-2(3))-(0) \\ =(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{27}{2}-6)=9+\frac{27}{2}-6=3+\frac{27}{2} \\ =\frac{6+27}{2}=\frac{33}{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We are given the functional equation:

$f(x^{2}+1)=x^{4}+5x^{2}+2$

Let $t=x^{2}+1$ . This implies that $x^{2}=t-1$ . Now, substitute this into the right side of the equation:

$\begin{aligned} f(t)=(t-1)^{2}+5(t-1)+2 \\ f(t)=(t^{2}-2t+1)+5t-5+2 \\ f(t)=t^{2}+3t-2 \end{aligned}$

Replacing $t$ back with $x$ , the polynomial function is:

$f(x)=x^{2}+3x-2$

Now, we calculate the definite integral from 0 to 3 :

$\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{3}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{3}(x^{2}+3x-2)dx \\ [\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{3x^{2}}{2}-2x]_{0}^{3} \\ =(\frac{3^{3}}{3}+\frac{3(3^{2})}{2}-2(3))-(0) \\ =(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{27}{2}-6)=9+\frac{27}{2}-6=3+\frac{27}{2} \\ =\frac{6+27}{2}=\frac{33}{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\pi+4x^{11}}{1-sin(|x|+\frac{\pi}{6})}+\frac{\pi-4x^{11}}{1-sin(|x|+\frac{\pi}{6})}dx \\ & =2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{1}{1-sin(x+\frac{\pi}{6})}dx \\ & =2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{1+sin(x+\frac{\pi}{6})}{cos^{2}(x+\frac{\pi}{6})}dx \\ & =2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}sec^{2}(x+\frac{\pi}{6})+tan(x+\frac{\pi}{6})sec(x+\frac{\pi}{6})dx \\ & \Rightarrow 2\pi[tan(x+\frac{\pi}{6})+sec(x+\frac{\pi}{6})]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ & \Rightarrow 4\pi \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}(y+xe^{x})f(y)dy$ , then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.question_html: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}(y+xe^{x})f(y)dy$ , then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}(y+xe^{x})f(y)dy \\ & f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy+\int_{0}^{1}xe^{x}f(y)dy \end{aligned}$ Integration is w.r.t $y$ , so variable $x$ is taken as a constant. $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy+xe^{x}\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy.$ Let $A=\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy$ and $B=\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy$ , both are constants. So $f(x)$ becomes, $f(x)=e^{x}+A+Bxe^{x}...(1)$ Or, $f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}...(2)$ Solve, $B=\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy$ . $B=\int_{0}^{1}[e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}]dy,{\text{from (2)}f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}}.$ $B=\int_{0}^{1}[e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}]dy\text{, {from (2)}f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}\text{}.}$ Using integration by parts, $\int ye^{y}dy=ye^{y}-\int e^{y}=e^{y}(y-1)$ . $\begin{aligned} & B=[e^{y}+Ay+Be^{y}(y-1)]_{0}^{1}. \\ & B=[e^{1}+A \cdot 1+0-e^{0}-0-B \cdot e^{0}(-1)]. \\ & B=e+A-1+B⟹A=1-e. \end{aligned}$ Finding $f(0)$ using equation (1). $\begin{aligned} & f(0)=1+A+0. \\ & f(0)=1+1-e,{\text{substitute}A=1-e}. \\ & f(0)+e=2 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}(y+xe^{x})f(y)dy \\ & f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy+\int_{0}^{1}xe^{x}f(y)dy \end{aligned}$

Integration is w.r.t $y$ , so variable $x$ is taken as a constant.

$f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy+xe^{x}\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy.$

Let $A=\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy$ and $B=\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy$ , both are constants.

So $f(x)$ becomes,

$f(x)=e^{x}+A+Bxe^{x}...(1)$

Or, $f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}...(2)$

Solve, $B=\int_{0}^{1}f(y)dy$ .

$B=\int_{0}^{1}[e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}]dy,{\text{from (2)}f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}}.$

$B=\int_{0}^{1}[e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}]dy\text{, {from (2)}f(y)=e^{y}+A+Bye^{y}\text{}.}$

Using integration by parts, $\int ye^{y}dy=ye^{y}-\int e^{y}=e^{y}(y-1)$ .

$\begin{aligned} & B=[e^{y}+Ay+Be^{y}(y-1)]_{0}^{1}. \\ & B=[e^{1}+A \cdot 1+0-e^{0}-0-B \cdot e^{0}(-1)]. \\ & B=e+A-1+B⟹A=1-e. \end{aligned}$

Finding $f(0)$ using equation (1).

$\begin{aligned} & f(0)=1+A+0. \\ & f(0)=1+1-e,{\text{substitute}A=1-e}. \\ & f(0)+e=2 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $[ \cdot ]$ denote the greatest integer function and $f(x)=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n^{3}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}[\frac{k^{2}}{3^{x}}]$ . Then $12\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}f(i)$ is equal to ________.
questions.question_html: Let $[ \cdot ]$ denote the greatest integer function and $f(x)=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n^{3}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}[\frac{k^{2}}{3^{x}}]$ . Then $12\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}f(i)$ is equal to ________.
questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}(\frac{1}{n^{3}} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{n}[\frac{k^{2}}{3^{x}}])=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n^{3}} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{n}(\frac{k^{2}}{3^{x}})-\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n^{3}} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{n}{\frac{k^{2}}{3^{x}}} \\ & f(x)=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n^{3}} \times \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6 \times 3^{x}}-0 \Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{1}{3^{x+1}} \\ & 12\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}f(j)=12(\frac{1}{3^{2}}+\frac{1}{3^{3}}+\frac{1}{3^{4}}+\dots.)=12(\frac{\frac{1}{9}}{1-\frac{1}{3}})=\frac{12}{9-3}=2 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The integral $\int_{-1}^{\frac{3}{2}}(|\pi^{2}xsin(\pi x)|)dx$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{Let,}I=\pi^{2}\int_{-1}^{3/2}|xsin\pi x|dx \\ & \begin{aligned} & =\pi^{2}{\int_{-1}^{1}xsin\pi xdx-\int_{1}^{3/2}xsin\pi xdx} \\ & =\pi^{2}{2\int_{0}^{1}xsin\pi xdx-\int_{-1}^{3/2}xsin\pi xdx} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Consider} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \int xsin\pi xdx \\ & -x \cdot \frac{1}{\pi}cos\pi x+\int 1 \cdot \frac{1}{\pi}cos\pi xdx \\ & =--\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}} \\ & I=\pi^{2}{2(-\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}})_{0}^{1}-(-\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}})_{1}^{3/2}} \\ & =\pi^{2}{\frac{2}{\pi}-(-\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}-\frac{1}{\pi})} \\ & =\pi^{2}{\frac{3}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}} \\ & =3\pi+1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{Let,}I=\pi^{2}\int_{-1}^{3/2}|xsin\pi x|dx \\ & \begin{aligned} & =\pi^{2}{\int_{-1}^{1}xsin\pi xdx-\int_{1}^{3/2}xsin\pi xdx} \\ & =\pi^{2}{2\int_{0}^{1}xsin\pi xdx-\int_{-1}^{3/2}xsin\pi xdx} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Consider} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \int xsin\pi xdx \\ & -x \cdot \frac{1}{\pi}cos\pi x+\int 1 \cdot \frac{1}{\pi}cos\pi xdx \\ & =--\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}} \\ & I=\pi^{2}{2(-\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}})_{0}^{1}-(-\frac{x}{\pi}cos\pi x+\frac{sin\pi x}{\pi^{2}})_{1}^{3/2}} \\ & =\pi^{2}{\frac{2}{\pi}-(-\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}-\frac{1}{\pi})} \\ & =\pi^{2}{\frac{3}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}} \\ & =3\pi+1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $f:R \rightarrow R$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(2)=1$ . If $F(x)=xf(x)$ for all $x \in R$ , $\int_{0}^{2}xF^{'}(x)dx=6$ and $\int_{0}^{2}x^{2}F^{''}(x)dx=40$ , then $F^{'}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}F(x)dx$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $f:R \rightarrow R$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(2)=1$ . If $F(x)=xf(x)$ for all $x \in R$ , $\int_{0}^{2}xF^{'}(x)dx=6$ and $\int_{0}^{2}x^{2}F^{''}(x)dx=40$ , then $F^{'}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}F(x)dx$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{2}xF^{'}(x)dx=6 \\ & =xF(x)|_{0}^{2}-\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx=6 \\ & =2F(2)-\int_{0}^{2}xF(x)dx=6[ \therefore f(2)=2F(2)=2] \\ & \int_{0}^{2}xF(x)dx=-2\dots(1) \\ & \Rightarrow \int_{0}^{2}F(x)dx=-2\dots(2) \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Also} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{2}x^{2}F^{''}(x)dx=x^{2}F^{'}(x)|_{0}^{2}-2\int_{0}^{2}xF^{'}(x)dx=40 \\ & =4F^{'}(2)-2 \times 6=40 \\ & F^{'}(2)=13 \\ & \therefore F^{'}(2)+\int_{0}^{2}F(x)=13-2=11 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let f(x) be a positive function and $I_{1}=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{1}2xf(2x(1-2x))dx$ and $I_{2}=\int_{-1}^{2}f(x(1-x))dx$ . Then the value of $\frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}$ is equal to ________
questions.question_html: Let f(x) be a positive function and $I_{1}=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{1}2xf(2x(1-2x))dx$ and $I_{2}=\int_{-1}^{2}f(x(1-x))dx$ . Then the value of $\frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}$ is equal to ________
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & I_{1}=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{1}2xf(2x(1-2x))dx \\ & \Rightarrow 2x=t \Rightarrow 2dx=dt \Rightarrow I_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{2}tf(t(1-t))dt \\ & \Rightarrow 2I_{1}=\int_{-1}^{2}(1-t)f(1-t)(1-(1-t))dt \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow 2I_{1}=\int_{-1}^{2}f(t(1-t)dt-\int_{-1}^{2}tf(t(1-t)dt$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2I_{1}=I_{2}-2I_{1} \\ & \Rightarrow 4I_{1}=I_{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}=4 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The integral $\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8xdx}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8x}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx\dots(1) \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8(\pi-x)}{4cos^{2}(\pi-x)+sin^{2}(\pi-x)}dx \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8(\pi-x)}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx\dots(2) \end{aligned}$ Adding (1) and (2) $\begin{aligned} & 2I=8\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{1}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx \\ & I=4\pi \times 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sec^{2}x}{4tan^{2}x}dx \end{aligned}$ Put $tanx=t$ $sec^{2}xdx=dt$ $I=8\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{4+t^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & I=8\pi\frac{1}{2}(tan^{-1}\frac{t}{2})_{0}^{\infty} \\ & I=4\pi(\frac{\pi}{2}) \\ & I=2\pi^{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8x}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx\dots(1) \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8(\pi-x)}{4cos^{2}(\pi-x)+sin^{2}(\pi-x)}dx \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{8(\pi-x)}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx\dots(2) \end{aligned}$

Adding (1) and (2)

$\begin{aligned} & 2I=8\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{1}{4cos^{2}x+sin^{2}x}dx \\ & I=4\pi \times 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sec^{2}x}{4tan^{2}x}dx \end{aligned}$

Put $tanx=t$

$sec^{2}xdx=dt$

$I=8\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{4+t^{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & I=8\pi\frac{1}{2}(tan^{-1}\frac{t}{2})_{0}^{\infty} \\ & I=4\pi(\frac{\pi}{2}) \\ & I=2\pi^{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $f:(0,\infty) \rightarrow R$ be a twice differentiable function. If for some $a \ne 0,\int_{0}^{1}f(\lambda x)d\lambda=af(x),f(1)=1$ and $f(16)=\frac{1}{8}$ , then $16-f^{'}(\frac{1}{16})$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let $f:(0,\infty) \rightarrow R$ be a twice differentiable function. If for some $a \ne 0,\int_{0}^{1}f(\lambda x)d\lambda=af(x),f(1)=1$ and $f(16)=\frac{1}{8}$ , then $16-f^{'}(\frac{1}{16})$ is equal to __________.

questions.question_html: The integral $\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(x+3)sinx}{1+3cos^{2}x}dx$ is equal to
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(x+3)sinx}{1+3cos^{2}x}dx\text{..... (i)} \\ & =\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x+3)sin(\pi-x)}{1+3cos^{2}(\pi-x)}dx \\ & =\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi+3)sinx-xsinx}{1+3cos^{2}x}dx\text{..... (ii)} \end{aligned}$

Add (i) & (ii)

$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi+6)sinx}{1+3cos^{2}x}dx$

Let $cosx=t \Rightarrow -sinxdx=dt$

$(\pi+6)\int_{1}^{-1}\frac{-dt}{(1+3t^{2})}=(\frac{\pi+6}{3})\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dt}{t^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow 2I=(\frac{\pi+6}{3}) \cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})} \cdot tan^{-1}\frac{t}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}|_{-1}^{1}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2I=(\frac{\pi+6}{\sqrt{3}})[tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})-tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3})] \\ & =(\frac{\pi+6}{\sqrt{3}}) \cdot (\frac{\pi}{3}-(-\frac{\pi}{3})) \\ & =(\frac{\pi+6}{\sqrt{3}}) \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi(\pi+6)}{3\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Ensure the innermost function is greater than zero:

$log_{6}(3+4x-x^{2})>1$

Step 2: Simplify the inequality from Step 1:

$3+4x-x^{2}>6⟹x^{2}-4x+3<0$

Step 3: Solve the quadratic inequality:

$(x-1)(x-3)<0$

This inequality indicates that $x$ must lie between the roots, giving the interval $x \in (1,3)$ .

With the domain of $f(x)$ identified as $(a,b)=(1,3)$ , we calculate the definite integral over $[0,b-a]$ :

Calculate the Integral:

Given:

$\int_{0}^{b-a}[x^{2}]dx$

For $b-a=2$ , we compute:

$\int_{1}^{2}[x^{2}]dx=\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}1dx+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}2dx+\int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2}3dx$

Computation of Each Integral Segment:

$\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}1dx=\sqrt{2}-1$

$\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}2dx=2(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})$

$\int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2}3dx=3(2-\sqrt{3})$

Summing these, we have:

$5-\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3}$

Conclusion:

The values for $p,q,$ and $r$ are $p=5$ , $q=2$ , and $r=3$ , with the greatest common divisor of these numbers being 1. Therefore, adding them together gives:

$p+q+r=5+2+3=10$

questions.question_html: Let for $f(x)=7tan^{8}x+7tan^{6}x-3tan^{4}x-3tan^{2}x,I_{1}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}f(x)dx$ and $I_{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}xf(x)dx$ . Then $7I_{1}+12I_{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =7tan^{8}x+7tan^{6}x-3tan^{4}x-3tan^{2}x \\ & =7tan^{6}x(1+tan^{2}x)-3tan^{2}x(1+tan^{2}x) \\ & =(7tan^{6}x-3tan^{2}x)(1+tan^{2}x) \\ & =(7tan^{6}x-3tan^{2}x)sec^{2}x \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} I_{1}= & \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(7tan^{6}x-3tan^{2}x)sec^{2}xdx \\ & =(\frac{7tan^{7}x}{7}-\frac{3tan^{3}x}{3})|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}=1-1=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} I_{2}= & \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}xf(x)dx=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}x(7tan^{6}x-3tan^{2}x)sec^{2}xdx \\ & =x(tan^{7}x-tan^{3}x)|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}-\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}1 \cdot (tan^{7}x-tan^{3}x)dx \\ & =0-\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}tan^{3}x(tan^{2}x-1)(tan^{2}x+1)dx \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(tan^{3}x-tan^{5}x)sec^{2}xdx=\frac{tan^{4}x}{4}-\frac{tan^{6}x}{6}|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ & =\frac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$

Hence $7I_{1}+12I_{2}=1$

questions.question_text: Let [.] denote the greatest integer function. If $\int_{0}^{e^{3}}[\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}]dx=\alpha-log_{e}2$ , then $\alpha^{3}$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: Let [.] denote the greatest integer function. If $\int_{0}^{e^{3}}[\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}]dx=\alpha-log_{e}2$ , then $\alpha^{3}$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: To solve this, we start by evaluating the integral: $I=\int_{0}^{e^{3}}[\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}]dx$ The greatest integer function $[ \cdot ]$ returns the largest integer less than or equal to the input value. Here's how we can approach the problem: Determine the function inside the integral : $\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}=e^{1-x}$ . Identifying the intervals : When $e^{1-x} \ge 2$ , which simplifies to $x \le 1-ln2$ , we have $[e^{1-x}]=2$ . When $1 \le e^{1-x}<2$ , simplifying gives $1-ln2<x \le 1$ , and thus $[e^{1-x}]=1$ . When $0 \le e^{1-x}<1$ , which holds for $x>1$ , thus $[e^{1-x}]=0$ from $x=1$ to $x=e^{3}$ . Evaluate the integral on these intervals : $\int_{0}^{1-ln2}2dx=2(1-ln2)$ $\int_{1-ln2}^{1}1dx=1-(1-ln2)=ln2$ $\int_{1}^{e^{3}}0dx=0$ Combine these results : $I=2(1-ln2)+ln2+0=2-ln2$ Thus, we are given that: $\alpha-ln2=2-ln2$ This implies that: $\alpha=2$ Therefore, $\alpha^{3}=2^{3}=8$ .

To solve this, we start by evaluating the integral:

$I=\int_{0}^{e^{3}}[\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}]dx$

The greatest integer function $[ \cdot ]$ returns the largest integer less than or equal to the input value. Here's how we can approach the problem:

Determine the function inside the integral:

$\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}=e^{1-x}$ .

Identifying the intervals:

When $e^{1-x} \ge 2$ , which simplifies to $x \le 1-ln2$ , we have $[e^{1-x}]=2$ .

When $1 \le e^{1-x}<2$ , simplifying gives $1-ln2<x \le 1$ , and thus $[e^{1-x}]=1$ .

When $0 \le e^{1-x}<1$ , which holds for $x>1$ , thus $[e^{1-x}]=0$ from $x=1$ to $x=e^{3}$ .

Evaluate the integral on these intervals:

$\int_{0}^{1-ln2}2dx=2(1-ln2)$

$\int_{1-ln2}^{1}1dx=1-(1-ln2)=ln2$

$\int_{1}^{e^{3}}0dx=0$

Combine these results:

$I=2(1-ln2)+ln2+0=2-ln2$

Thus, we are given that:

$\alpha-ln2=2-ln2$

This implies that:

$\alpha=2$

Therefore, $\alpha^{3}=2^{3}=8$ .

questions.question_html: Let $f(x)+2f(\frac{1}{x})=x^{2}+5$ and $2g(x)-3g(\frac{1}{x})=x,x>0$ . If $\alpha=\int_{1}^{2}f(x)dx$ , and $\beta=\int_{1}^{2}g(x)dx$ , then the value of $9\alpha+\beta$ is :
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & f(x)+2f(\frac{1}{x})=x^{2}+5 \\ & 2f(\frac{1}{x})+4f(x)=2(\frac{1}{x^{2}}+5) \\ & 3f(x)=\frac{2}{x^{2}}-x^{2}+5 \\ & f(x)=\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x^{2}}-x^{2}+5) \\ & 2g(x)-3g(\frac{1}{x})=x \\ & 2g(\frac{1}{x})-3g(x)=\frac{1}{x} \\ & \text{Or}4g(x)-6g(\frac{1}{x})=2x \\ & 6g(\frac{1}{x})-9g(x)=\frac{3}{x} \\ & -5g(x)=2x+\frac{3}{x} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $f:[1,\infty) \rightarrow [2,\infty)$ be a differentiable function. If $10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$ for all $x⩾1$ , then the value of $f(3)$ is :
questions.question_html: Let $f:[1,\infty) \rightarrow [2,\infty)$ be a differentiable function. If $10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$ for all $x⩾1$ , then the value of $f(3)$ is :
questions.explanation_text: To solve the problem, we start with the given equation: $10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$ By differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we have: $\frac{d}{dx}(10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt)=\frac{d}{dx}(5xf(x)-x^{5}-9)$ The left side simplifies to $10f(x)$ . For the right side, using the product rule and the power rule, we get: $10f(x)=5f(x)+5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$ Rearranging terms, we obtain: $5f(x)=5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$ Let $y=f(x)$ . Thus: $5y=5x\frac{dy}{dx}-5x^{4}$ Dividing by 5, we have: $y=x\frac{dy}{dx}-x^{4}$ Rewriting, we get: $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x}=x^{3}$ This is a linear differential equation. The integrating factor (I.F.) is calculated as: $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{-1}{x}dx}=e^{-lnx}=\frac{1}{x}$ Multiplying through by the integrating factor, we have: $y \cdot \frac{1}{x}=\int x^{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x}dx=\int x^{2}dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$ Thus, we solve for $y$ : $y=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+Cx$ Substituting back, we need to find $C$ using the condition at $x=1$ : Since $\int_{1}^{1}f(t)dt=0$ , we substitute: $10 \cdot 0=5 \cdot 1 \cdot f(1)-1^{5}-9 \Rightarrow 0=5f(1)-1-9$ $5f(1)=10 \Rightarrow f(1)=2$ Now use $f(1)=2$ in the function: $2=\frac{1}{3}+C \cdot 1 \Rightarrow C=\frac{5}{3}$ The function $f(x)$ is given by: $f(x)=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}x$ To find $f(3)$ : $f(3)=\frac{3^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3} \cdot 3=27+5=32$ Therefore, the value of $f(3)$ is 32.
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the problem, we start with the given equation:

$10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$

By differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we have:

$\frac{d}{dx}(10\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt)=\frac{d}{dx}(5xf(x)-x^{5}-9)$

The left side simplifies to $10f(x)$ . For the right side, using the product rule and the power rule, we get:

$10f(x)=5f(x)+5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$

Rearranging terms, we obtain:

$5f(x)=5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$

Let $y=f(x)$ . Thus:

$5y=5x\frac{dy}{dx}-5x^{4}$

Dividing by 5, we have:

$y=x\frac{dy}{dx}-x^{4}$

Rewriting, we get:

$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x}=x^{3}$

This is a linear differential equation. The integrating factor (I.F.) is calculated as:

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{-1}{x}dx}=e^{-lnx}=\frac{1}{x}$

Multiplying through by the integrating factor, we have:

$y \cdot \frac{1}{x}=\int x^{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x}dx=\int x^{2}dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$

Thus, we solve for $y$ :

$y=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+Cx$

Substituting back, we need to find $C$ using the condition at $x=1$ :

Since $\int_{1}^{1}f(t)dt=0$ , we substitute:

$10 \cdot 0=5 \cdot 1 \cdot f(1)-1^{5}-9 \Rightarrow 0=5f(1)-1-9$

$5f(1)=10 \Rightarrow f(1)=2$

Now use $f(1)=2$ in the function:

$2=\frac{1}{3}+C \cdot 1 \Rightarrow C=\frac{5}{3}$

The function $f(x)$ is given by:

$f(x)=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}x$

To find $f(3)$ :

$f(3)=\frac{3^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3} \cdot 3=27+5=32$

Therefore, the value of $f(3)$ is 32.

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & f(t)=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{2xdx}{1-cos^{2}tsin^{2}x} \\ & x \rightarrow \pi-x \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & f(t)=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{2(\pi-x)dx}{1-cos^{2}tsin^{2}x}=2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1-cos^{2}tsin^{2}x}-f(t) \\ & \Rightarrow f(t)=\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1-cos^{2}tsin^{2}x} \\ & =2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{dx}{1-cos^{2}tsin^{2}x} \\ & f(t)=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sec^{2}xdx}{sec^{2}x-cos^{2}ttan^{2}x} \\ & I_{1}=\int \frac{sec^{2}xdx}{sec^{2}x-cos^{2}ttan^{2}x} \\ & \text{Put}costtanx=\lambda \Rightarrow costsec^{2}xdx=d\lambda \\ & I_{1}=\int \frac{d\lambda}{cost \cdot (1+\lambda^{2}sec^{2}t-\lambda^{2})}=\int \frac{d\lambda}{cost(1+\lambda^{2}tan^{2}t)} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} =\frac{1}{cost \cdot tan^{2}t} \cdot \int \frac{d\lambda}{\lambda^{2}+cos^{2}t}= & \frac{1}{costtan^{2}t} \\ & \times \frac{1}{cost}tan^{-1}(\lambda tant) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{sint}tan^{-1}(sinttanx) \\ \Rightarrow & f(t)=\frac{2\pi}{sint}tan^{-1}(sinttanx)]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{sint} \\ \Rightarrow & \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{\pi^{2}dt}{f(t)}=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sintdt=1 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosxdx}{(1+e^{sinx})(1+sin^{4}x)}=\alpha\pi+\beta log_{e}(3+2\sqrt{2})$ , where $\alpha,\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{(1+e^{sinx})(1+sin^{4}x)}dx$ ............(1) Apply king's rule $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx(e^{sinx})}{(1+e^{sinx})(1+sin^{4}x)}dx$ ..........(2) Adding (1) and (2), we get $\begin{aligned} & 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1+sin^{4}x}dx \\ \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1+sin^{4}x}dx, \end{aligned}$ Let $sinx=t$ $\begin{aligned} & I=8\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dt}{1+t^{4}} \\ \\ & =4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})-(1-\frac{1}{t^{2}})}{t^{2}+\frac{1}{t^{2}}}dt \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})dt}{(t-\frac{1}{t^{2}})^{2}+2}-4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-\frac{1}{t^{2}})dt}{(t+\frac{1}{t^{2}})^{2}-2} \\ \\ & =4\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⎛⎝tan^{-1}\frac{t-\frac{1}{t}}{\sqrt{2}}|_{0}^{1}-4\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[log|\frac{t+\frac{1}{t}-\sqrt{2}}{t+\frac{1}{t}+\sqrt{2}}|]_{0}^{1} \\ \\ & =2\pi-2log|\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}| \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =2\pi+2log(3+2\sqrt{2})=\alpha\pi+\beta log_{e}(3+2\sqrt{2}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2,\beta=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{(1+e^{sinx})(1+sin^{4}x)}dx$ ............(1)

Apply king's rule

$I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx(e^{sinx})}{(1+e^{sinx})(1+sin^{4}x)}dx$ ..........(2)

Adding (1) and (2), we get

$\begin{aligned} & 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1+sin^{4}x}dx \\ \\ & I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{8\sqrt{2}cosx}{1+sin^{4}x}dx, \end{aligned}$

Let $sinx=t$

$\begin{aligned} & I=8\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dt}{1+t^{4}} \\ \\ & =4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})-(1-\frac{1}{t^{2}})}{t^{2}+\frac{1}{t^{2}}}dt \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})dt}{(t-\frac{1}{t^{2}})^{2}+2}-4\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-\frac{1}{t^{2}})dt}{(t+\frac{1}{t^{2}})^{2}-2} \\ \\ & =4\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⎛⎝tan^{-1}\frac{t-\frac{1}{t}}{\sqrt{2}}|_{0}^{1}-4\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[log|\frac{t+\frac{1}{t}-\sqrt{2}}{t+\frac{1}{t}+\sqrt{2}}|]_{0}^{1} \\ \\ & =2\pi-2log|\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}| \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =2\pi+2log(3+2\sqrt{2})=\alpha\pi+\beta log_{e}(3+2\sqrt{2}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2,\beta=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$
