questions.question_html:
A value of $\alpha$ such that
$\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+1}\frac{dx}{(x+\alpha)(x+\alpha+1)}=log_{e}(\frac{9}{8})$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $I=\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+1}\frac{dx}{(x+\alpha)(x+\alpha+1)}$ Let x + $\alpha$ = t and dx = dt $I=\int_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}\frac{dt}{t(t+1)}=\int_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{t+1})dx$ $\Rightarrow (lnt-ln(t+1))|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}=ln(\frac{t}{t+1})|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}$ $\Rightarrow ln(\frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha+2})-ln(\frac{2\alpha}{2\alpha+1})$ $\Rightarrow ln(\frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha+2} \times \frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha})=ln(\frac{9}{8})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(2\alpha+1)^{2}}{(2\alpha+2)}=\frac{9\alpha}{4}$ $4(4\alpha^{2}+1+4\alpha)=18\alpha^{2}+18\alpha$ $\Rightarrow 2\alpha^{2}-2\alpha-4=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\alpha-2=0$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha+2)(\alpha-1)=0$ $\alpha$ = 1 or $\alpha$ = -2
questions.explanation_html:
$I=\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+1}\frac{dx}{(x+\alpha)(x+\alpha+1)}$

Let x + $\alpha$ = t and dx = dt

$I=\int_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}\frac{dt}{t(t+1)}=\int_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{t+1})dx$

$\Rightarrow (lnt-ln(t+1))|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}=ln(\frac{t}{t+1})|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha+1}$

$\Rightarrow ln(\frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha+2})-ln(\frac{2\alpha}{2\alpha+1})$

$\Rightarrow ln(\frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha+2} \times \frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha})=ln(\frac{9}{8})$

$\Rightarrow \frac{(2\alpha+1)^{2}}{(2\alpha+2)}=\frac{9\alpha}{4}$

$4(4\alpha^{2}+1+4\alpha)=18\alpha^{2}+18\alpha$

$\Rightarrow 2\alpha^{2}-2\alpha-4=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\alpha-2=0$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha+2)(\alpha-1)=0$

$\alpha$ = 1 or $\alpha$ = -2

questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}\frac{x}{1+sinx}dx$ also let K = $\frac{x}{1+sinx}$ Multiplying numerator and denominator by (1 $-$ sin x) we get; $K=\frac{x(1-sinx)}{1-(sinx)^{2}}=\frac{x(1-sinx)}{(cosx)^{2}}$ = x(1 $-$ sin x) sec 2 x = x sec 2 x $-$ x sin x sec 2 x = x sec 2 x $-$ x tan x sec x Now, $I=\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}xsec^{2}xdx-\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}xsecxtanxdx$ $\Rightarrow$ I = $|xtanx|_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}-[log(secx)]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}$ - $|\frac{x}{cosx}|_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}-\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}\frac{dx}{cosx}$ $\Rightarrow$ I = $|xtanx|_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}$ - $|\frac{x}{cosx}|_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}$ $-[log(secx+tanx)]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}$ $\Rightarrow$ I = $-\frac{3\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}$ $+\frac{3\pi}{4}(\sqrt{2})$ $+\frac{\pi}{4}(\sqrt{2})$ $-log(\sqrt{2}+1)$ $+log(\sqrt{2}+1)$ $\Rightarrow$ I = - $\pi$ + $\sqrt{2}\pi$ $\Rightarrow$ I = $\pi(\sqrt{2}-1)$

questions.question_html: The value of $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}dx$ is
questions.explanation_text: As we know, $\int_{a}^{b}+(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$ Let $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}dx$ $\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}(-\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}-x)}{1+2^{-\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}-x}}$ $\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{-x}}dx$ $\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{2^{x}sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}dx$ $\therefore$ $2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}+\frac{2^{x}sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}})dx$ $\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}x(\frac{1+2^{x}}{1+2^{x}})dx$ $\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ $\Rightarrow 2I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ [ as sin 2 x is an even function ] $\Rightarrow I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ [ as $\int_{0}^{a}f(a)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx]$ So, $I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}(\frac{b}{2}-x)dx$ $I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$ $\therefore$ $2I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(sin^{2}x+cos^{2}x)dx$ $\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}dx$ $\Rightarrow 2I=[x]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ $\Rightarrow 2I=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
As we know,

$\int_{a}^{b}+(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$

Let $I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}dx$

$\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}(-\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}-x)}{1+2^{-\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}-x}}$

$\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{-x}}dx$

$\Rightarrow I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{2^{x}sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}dx$

$\therefore$ $2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\frac{sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}}+\frac{2^{x}sin^{2}x}{1+2^{x}})dx$

$\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}x(\frac{1+2^{x}}{1+2^{x}})dx$

$\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$

$\Rightarrow 2I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ [ as sin2 x is an even function ]

$\Rightarrow I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$

[ as $\int_{0}^{a}f(a)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx]$

So, $I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}(\frac{b}{2}-x)dx$

$I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$

$\therefore$ $2I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(sin^{2}x+cos^{2}x)dx$

$\Rightarrow 2I=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}dx$

$\Rightarrow 2I=[x]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$

$\Rightarrow 2I=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi}{4}$

questions.question_html:
The value of the integral

$\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1+log(\frac{2+sinx}{2-sinx}))dx$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let I = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1+log(\frac{2+sinx}{2-sinx}))dx$ ......(1) $\Rightarrow$ I = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}(-x)(1+log(\frac{2+sin(-x)}{2-sin(-x)}))dx$ [ As $\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$ ] = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1+log(\frac{2-sinx}{2+sinx}))dx$ = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1-log(\frac{2+sinx}{2-sinx}))dx$ .......(2) Adding equation (1) and (2) we get, 2I = 2 $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$ 2I = 4 $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$ I = 2 $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$ = $\frac{2 \times \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \pi}{2 \times 2}$ [ Using Gamma function ] = $\frac{3\pi}{8}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let

I = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1+log(\frac{2+sinx}{2-sinx}))dx$ ......(1)

$\Rightarrow$ I = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}(-x)(1+log(\frac{2+sin(-x)}{2-sin(-x)}))dx$

[ As $\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$ ]

     = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1+log(\frac{2-sinx}{2+sinx}))dx$

     = $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}x(1-log(\frac{2+sinx}{2-sinx}))dx$ .......(2)

Adding equation (1) and (2) we get,

2I = 2 $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$

2I = 4 $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$

I = 2 $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{4}xdx$

  = $\frac{2 \times \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \pi}{2 \times 2}$ [ Using Gamma function ]

  = $\frac{3\pi}{8}$

questions.question_html:
If    $\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1^{a}+2^{a}+......+n^{a}}{(n+1)^{a-1}[(na+1)+(na+2)+.....+(na+n)]}=\frac{1}{60}$

for some positive real number a, then a is equal to :
questions.explanation_html:
$\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{\frac{1}{(a+1)}.n^{a+1}+a_{1}n^{a}+a_{2}n^{a-1}+....}{(n+1)^{a-1}.n^{2}(a+\frac{1+\frac{1}{n}}{2})}=\frac{1}{60}$

$\Rightarrow$    $\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{(\frac{1}{n})^{2}+(\frac{2}{n})^{a}+.......+(\frac{n}{n})^{a}}{(n+1)^{a-1}[a^{2}a+\frac{n(n+1)}{2}]}=\frac{1}{60}$

         $=\frac{\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}(\frac{r}{n})^{a}}{(1+\frac{1}{n})^{a-1}[a+\frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{1}{n})]}=\frac{1}{60}$

         $=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}x^{a}dx}{(a+\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{60}=\frac{\frac{1}{a+1}}{a+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{60}$

$\Rightarrow$    $\frac{\frac{1}{a+1}}{(a+\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{60} \Rightarrow (a+1)(2a+1)=120$

$\Rightarrow$   2a2 + 3a $-$ 119 $=$ 0

$\Rightarrow$    2a2 + 17a $-$ 14a $-$ 119 $=$ 0

$\Rightarrow$    (a $-$ 7) (2a + 17) $=$ 0

$\Rightarrow$    a $=$ 7, $-$ $\frac{17}{2}$

questions.question_html: If    $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{(x^{2}-2x+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{k}{k+5},$ then k is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given, I = $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{(x^{2}-2x+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ = $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{[(x-1)^{2}+3]^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ Let x $-$ 1 = $\sqrt{3}$ tan $\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ dx = $\sqrt{3}$ sec 2 $\theta$ d $\theta$ When x = 1, then $\theta$ = 0 and when x = 2, $\theta$ = $\frac{\pi}{6}$ I = $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{(3tan^{2}\theta+3)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ = $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{(3sec^{2}\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ = $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{3\sqrt{3}sec^{3}\theta}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{d\theta}{sec\theta}$ = $\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}cos\theta d\theta$ = $\frac{1}{3}[sin\theta]_{\theta}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$ = $\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$ $\therefore$ According to the question, $\frac{k}{k+5}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$ $\Rightarrow$ 6k = k + 5 $\Rightarrow$ k = 1
questions.explanation_html:
Given, I = $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{(x^{2}-2x+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

= $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{[(x-1)^{2}+3]^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

Let x $-$ 1 = $\sqrt{3}$ tan $\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ dx = $\sqrt{3}$ sec2 $\theta$ d $\theta$

When x = 1, then $\theta$ = 0

and when x = 2, $\theta$ = $\frac{\pi}{6}$

I = $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{(3tan^{2}\theta+3)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

= $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{(3sec^{2}\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

= $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{\sqrt{3}sec^{2}\theta d\theta}{3\sqrt{3}sec^{3}\theta}$

= $\frac{1}{3}$ $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{d\theta}{sec\theta}$

= $\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}cos\theta d\theta$

= $\frac{1}{3}[sin\theta]_{\theta}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$

= $\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}$

= $\frac{1}{6}$

$\therefore$ According to the question,

$\frac{k}{k+5}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$

$\Rightarrow$ 6k = k + 5

$\Rightarrow$ k = 1

questions.question_html: The integral $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8cos2x}{(tanx+cotx)^{3}}dx$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: tan x  +  cot x = $\frac{sinx}{cosx}$ + $\frac{cosx}{sinx}$ = $\frac{sin^{2}x+cos^{2}x}{sinxcosx}$ = $\frac{1}{sinxcosx}$ = $\frac{2}{sin2x}$ $\therefore$ $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8cos2x}{(tanx+cotx)^{3}}dx$ = $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8cos2x}{(\frac{2}{sin2x})^{3}}dx$ = $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8sin^{3}2x.cos2x}{8}dx$ = $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}sin^{3}2x.cos2xdx$ Let sin 2x = t $\Rightarrow$ 2 cos2x dx = dt At    x = $\frac{\pi}{12}$ , t = sin $\frac{\pi}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ At   x = $\frac{\pi}{4}$ , t = sin $\frac{\pi}{2}$ = 1. = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}t^{3}.dt$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $[\frac{t^{4}}{4}]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ $\frac{1}{4}$ $\times$ [ 1 4 $-$ ( $\frac{1}{2}$ ) 4 ] = $\frac{1}{8}$ $\times$ $\frac{15}{16}$ = $\frac{15}{128}$
questions.explanation_html:
tan x  +  cot x

= $\frac{sinx}{cosx}$ + $\frac{cosx}{sinx}$

= $\frac{sin^{2}x+cos^{2}x}{sinxcosx}$

= $\frac{1}{sinxcosx}$

= $\frac{2}{sin2x}$

$\therefore$ $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8cos2x}{(tanx+cotx)^{3}}dx$

= $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8cos2x}{(\frac{2}{sin2x})^{3}}dx$

= $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\frac{8sin^{3}2x.cos2x}{8}dx$

= $\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}sin^{3}2x.cos2xdx$

Let sin 2x = t

$\Rightarrow$ 2 cos2x dx = dt

At    x = $\frac{\pi}{12}$ , t = sin $\frac{\pi}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$

At   x = $\frac{\pi}{4}$ , t = sin $\frac{\pi}{2}$ = 1.

= $\frac{1}{2}$ $\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}t^{3}.dt$

= $\frac{1}{2}$ $[\frac{t^{4}}{4}]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}$

= $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ $\frac{1}{4}$ $\times$ [ 14 $-$ ( $\frac{1}{2}$ )4]

= $\frac{1}{8}$ $\times$ $\frac{15}{16}$ = $\frac{15}{128}$

x $\int_{1}^{x}y$ (t) dt = (x + 1) $\int_{1}^{x}ty$ (t) dt,  then y (x) equals :

questions.explanation_text: $x\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt=x\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt$ Differentiate w.r. to x. $\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt+x[y(x)-y(1)]$ $=\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+x[xy(x)-y(1)]+xy(x)-y(1)$ $\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt=\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+x^{2}y(x)-y(1)$ Diff. again w.r.t to x $y(x)-y(a)=xy(x)-y(a)+2xy(x)+x^{2}y^{3}(x)$ $(1-3x)y(x)=x^{2}y^{3}(x)$ $\frac{y^{3}(x)}{y(x)}=\frac{1-3x}{x^{2}}$ $\frac{1dy}{ydx}=\frac{1-3x}{x^{2}} \Rightarrow lny=-\frac{1}{x}-3lnx$ $ln(yx^{3})=-\frac{1}{x}$ $yx^{3}=-e^{-1/x}$ $y=\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}$ or $y=\frac{ce^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}$
questions.explanation_html:
$x\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt=x\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt$

Differentiate w.r. to x.

$\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt+x[y(x)-y(1)]$

$=\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+x[xy(x)-y(1)]+xy(x)-y(1)$

$\int_{1}^{x}y(t)dt=\int_{1}^{x}ty(t)dt+x^{2}y(x)-y(1)$

Diff. again w.r.t to x

$y(x)-y(a)=xy(x)-y(a)+2xy(x)+x^{2}y^{3}(x)$
$(1-3x)y(x)=x^{2}y^{3}(x)$

$\frac{y^{3}(x)}{y(x)}=\frac{1-3x}{x^{2}}$

$\frac{1dy}{ydx}=\frac{1-3x}{x^{2}} \Rightarrow lny=-\frac{1}{x}-3lnx$

$ln(yx^{3})=-\frac{1}{x}$

$yx^{3}=-e^{-1/x}$

$y=\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}$

or    $y=\frac{ce^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}$

questions.question_html: The value of $\int_{0}^{1}\frac{8log(1+x)}{1+x^{2}}dx$ is
questions.explanation_text: $I=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{8log(1+x)}{1+x^{2}}dx$ put $x=tan\theta,$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=sec^{2}\theta \Rightarrow dx=sec^{2}\theta d\theta$ $\therefore$ $I=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\frac{log(1+tan\theta)}{1+tan^{2}\theta}.sec^{2}\theta d\theta$ $I=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log(1+tan\theta)d\theta...(i)$ $=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[1+tan(\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta)]d\theta$ $=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[1+\frac{1-tan\theta}{1+tan\theta}]d\theta$ $=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[\frac{2}{1+tan\theta}]d\theta$ $=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}[log2-log(1+tan\theta)]d\theta$ $I=8.(log2)[x]_{0}^{\pi/4}-8$ $\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log(1+tan\theta)d\theta$ $I=8.\frac{\pi}{4}.log2-I$ $[$ From equation $(i)$ $]$ $\Rightarrow 2I=2\pi log2,$ $\therefore$ $I=\pi log2$
questions.explanation_html:
$I=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{8log(1+x)}{1+x^{2}}dx$

put $x=tan\theta,$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=sec^{2}\theta \Rightarrow dx=sec^{2}\theta d\theta$

$\therefore$ $I=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\frac{log(1+tan\theta)}{1+tan^{2}\theta}.sec^{2}\theta d\theta$

$I=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log(1+tan\theta)d\theta...(i)$

$=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[1+tan(\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta)]d\theta$

$=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[1+\frac{1-tan\theta}{1+tan\theta}]d\theta$

$=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log[\frac{2}{1+tan\theta}]d\theta$

$=8\int_{0}^{\pi/4}[log2-log(1+tan\theta)]d\theta$

$I=8.(log2)[x]_{0}^{\pi/4}-8$

$\int_{0}^{\pi/4}log(1+tan\theta)d\theta$

$I=8.\frac{\pi}{4}.log2-I$ $[$ From equation $(i)$ $]$

$\Rightarrow 2I=2\pi log2,$

$\therefore$ $I=\pi log2$

questions.question_text: Let $I=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx$ and $J=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx.$ Then which one of the following is true?
questions.question_html: Let $I=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx$ and $J=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx.$ Then which one of the following is true?
questions.explanation_text: We know that $\frac{sinx}{x}<1,$ for $x \in (0,1)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}<\sqrt{x}$ on $x \in (0,1)$ $\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{x}dx=[\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3}]_{0}^{1}$ $\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow I<\frac{2}{3}$ Also $\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ for $x \in (0,1)$ $\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\int_{0}^{1}x^{-1/2}dx$ $=[2\sqrt{x}]_{0}^{1}=2$ $\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<2$ $\Rightarrow J<2$
questions.explanation_html:
We know that $\frac{sinx}{x}<1,$ for $x \in (0,1)$

$\Rightarrow \frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}<\sqrt{x}$ on $x \in (0,1)$

$\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{x}dx=[\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3}]_{0}^{1}$

$\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{sinx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow I<\frac{2}{3}$

Also $\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ for $x \in (0,1)$

$\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<\int_{0}^{1}x^{-1/2}dx$

$=[2\sqrt{x}]_{0}^{1}=2$

$\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}\frac{cosx}{\sqrt{x}}dx<2$

$\Rightarrow J<2$

questions.explanation_text: $\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{x}\frac{dt}{t\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\therefore$ $[sec^{-1}t]_{\sqrt{2}}^{x}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $[$ As $\int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}=sec^{-1}x$ $]$ $\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x-sec^{-1}\sqrt{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x=sec\frac{3\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x=-\sqrt{2}$

$\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{x}\frac{dt}{t\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\therefore$ $[sec^{-1}t]_{\sqrt{2}}^{x}=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$[$ As $\int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}=sec^{-1}x$ $]$

$\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x-sec^{-1}\sqrt{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\Rightarrow sec^{-1}x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$

$\Rightarrow x=sec\frac{3\pi}{4}$

questions.question_html: Let $F(x)=f(x)+f(\frac{1}{x}),$ where $f(x)=\int_{l}^{x}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt,$ Then $F(e)$ equals
questions.explanation_text: Given $f(x)=f(x)+f(\frac{1}{x}),$ where $f(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt$ $\therefore$ $F(e)=f(e)+f(\frac{1}{e})$ $\Rightarrow F(e)$ $=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt+\int_{1}^{1/e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt....(A)$ Now for solving, $I=\int_{1}^{1/e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt$ $\therefore$ Put $\frac{1}{t}=z \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{t^{2}}dt=dz$ $\Rightarrow dt=-\frac{dz}{z^{2}}$ and limit for $t=1 \Rightarrow z=1$ and for $t=1/e \Rightarrow z=e$ $\therefore$ $I=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{log(\frac{1}{z})}{1+\frac{1}{z}}(-\frac{dz}{z^{2}})$ $=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{(log1-logz).z}{z+1}(-\frac{dz}{z^{2}})$ $=\int_{1}^{e}-\frac{logz}{(z+1)}(-\frac{dz}{z})$ [ as $log1=0$ ] $=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logz}{z(z+1)}dz$ $\therefore$ $I=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t(t+1)}dt$ $[$ By property $\int_{a}^{b}f(t)dt$ $=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx$ $]$ Equation $(A)$ becomes $F(e)=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt+\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t(1+t)}dt$ $=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{t.logt+logt}{t(1+t)}dt$ $=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{(logt)(t+1)}{t(1+t)}$ $\Rightarrow F(e)=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t}dt$ Let $logt=x$ $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{t}dt=dx$ $[$ for limit $t=1,x=0$ and $t=e,x=loge=1$ $]$ $\therefore$ $F(e)=\int_{0}^{1}xdx$ $\Rightarrow F(e)=[\frac{x^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{1}$ $\Rightarrow F(e)=\frac{1}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $f(x)=f(x)+f(\frac{1}{x}),$

where $f(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt$

$\therefore$ $F(e)=f(e)+f(\frac{1}{e})$

$\Rightarrow F(e)$

$=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt+\int_{1}^{1/e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt....(A)$

Now for solving, $I=\int_{1}^{1/e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt$

$\therefore$ Put $\frac{1}{t}=z \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{t^{2}}dt=dz$

$\Rightarrow dt=-\frac{dz}{z^{2}}$

and limit for $t=1 \Rightarrow z=1$ and for

$t=1/e \Rightarrow z=e$

$\therefore$ $I=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{log(\frac{1}{z})}{1+\frac{1}{z}}(-\frac{dz}{z^{2}})$

$=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{(log1-logz).z}{z+1}(-\frac{dz}{z^{2}})$

$=\int_{1}^{e}-\frac{logz}{(z+1)}(-\frac{dz}{z})$

[ as $log1=0$ ]

$=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logz}{z(z+1)}dz$

$\therefore$ $I=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t(t+1)}dt$

$[$ By property $\int_{a}^{b}f(t)dt$

$=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx$ $]$

Equation $(A)$ becomes

$F(e)=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{1+t}dt+\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t(1+t)}dt$

$=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{t.logt+logt}{t(1+t)}dt$

$=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{(logt)(t+1)}{t(1+t)}$

$\Rightarrow F(e)=\int_{1}^{e}\frac{logt}{t}dt$

Let $logt=x$

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{t}dt=dx$

$[$ for limit $t=1,x=0$

and $t=e,x=loge=1$ $]$

$\therefore$ $F(e)=\int_{0}^{1}xdx$

$\Rightarrow F(e)=[\frac{x^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{1}$

$\Rightarrow F(e)=\frac{1}{2}$

questions.question_html: The value of $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}}{1+a^{x}}dx,a>0,$ is
questions.explanation_text: Let $I=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}x}{1+a^{x}}dx...(1)$ $=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}(-x)}{1+a^{-x}}dx$ $[$ Using $\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$ $]$ $=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}x}{1+\alpha^{x}}dx...(2)$ Adding equations $(1)$ and $(2)$ we get $2I=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}cos^{2}x(\frac{1+a^{x}}{1+a^{x}})dx$ $=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}cos^{2}xdx$ $=2\int_{0}^{\pi}cos^{2}xdx$ $=2 \times 2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$ $=4\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ $\Rightarrow I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$ $=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(1-cos^{2}xdx)$ $\Rightarrow I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}dx-2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$ $\Rightarrow I+I=2(\frac{\pi}{2})=\pi$ $\Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $I=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}x}{1+a^{x}}dx...(1)$

$=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}(-x)}{1+a^{-x}}dx$

$[$ Using $\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)dx$ $]$

$=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{cos^{2}x}{1+\alpha^{x}}dx...(2)$

Adding equations $(1)$ and $(2)$ we get

$2I=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}cos^{2}x(\frac{1+a^{x}}{1+a^{x}})dx$

$=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}cos^{2}xdx$

$=2\int_{0}^{\pi}cos^{2}xdx$

$=2 \times 2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$

$=4\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$

$\Rightarrow I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}sin^{2}xdx$

$=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(1-cos^{2}xdx)$

$\Rightarrow I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}dx-2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}cos^{2}xdx$

$\Rightarrow I+I=2(\frac{\pi}{2})=\pi$

$\Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$=\pi.2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(sinx)dx$

$\therefore$ $I=\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(sinx)dx$

$\Rightarrow A=\pi$

questions.question_html: $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{2x(1+sinx)}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$ is
questions.explanation_text: $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{2x(1+sinx)}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$ $=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{2xdx}{1+cos^{2}x}+2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{xsinx}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$ $=0+4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{xsinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x};$ $[$ as $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx=0$ $]$ if $f(x)$ is odd $=2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx$ if $f(x)$ is even. $I=4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x)sin(\pi-x)}{1+cos^{2}(\pi-x)}dx$ $I=4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x)sinx}{1+cos^{2}x}$ $\Rightarrow I=4\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x}-4\int \frac{xsinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x}$ $\Rightarrow 2I=4\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sinx}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$ put $cosx=t \Rightarrow -sinxdx=dt$ $\therefore$ $I=-2\pi\int_{1}^{-1}\frac{1}{1+t^{2}}dt$ $=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+t^{2}}dt$ $=2\pi[tan^{-1}t]_{-1}^{1}$ $=2\pi[tan^{-1}1-tan^{-1}(-1)]$ $=2\pi[\frac{\pi}{4}-(\frac{-\pi}{4})]=2\pi\frac{\pi}{2}=\pi^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{2x(1+sinx)}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$

$=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{2xdx}{1+cos^{2}x}+2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{xsinx}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$

$=0+4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{xsinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x};$

$[$ as $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx=0$ $]$

if $f(x)$ is odd

$=2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx$ if $f(x)$ is even.

$I=4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x)sin(\pi-x)}{1+cos^{2}(\pi-x)}dx$

$I=4\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x)sinx}{1+cos^{2}x}$

$\Rightarrow I=4\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x}-4\int \frac{xsinxdx}{1+cos^{2}x}$

$\Rightarrow 2I=4\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{sinx}{1+cos^{2}x}dx$

put $cosx=t \Rightarrow -sinxdx=dt$

$\therefore$ $I=-2\pi\int_{1}^{-1}\frac{1}{1+t^{2}}dt$

$=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+t^{2}}dt$

$=2\pi[tan^{-1}t]_{-1}^{1}$

$=2\pi[tan^{-1}1-tan^{-1}(-1)]$

$=2\pi[\frac{\pi}{4}-(\frac{-\pi}{4})]=2\pi\frac{\pi}{2}=\pi^{2}$

questions.question_html: $I_{n}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}tan^{n}xdx$ then $\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}n[I_{n}+I_{n+2}]$ equals
questions.explanation_html:
$I_{n}+I_{n+2}$

$=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}tan^{n}x(1+tan^{2}x)dx$

$=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}tan^{n}xsec^{2}xdx$

$=[\frac{tan^{n+1}x}{n+1}]_{0}^{\pi/4}$

$=\frac{1-0}{n+1}=\frac{1}{n+1}$

$\therefore$ $I_{n}+I_{n+2}=\frac{1}{n+1}$

$\Rightarrow \underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}n[I_{n}+I_{n+2}]$

$=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}n.\frac{1}{n+1}=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{n}{n+1}$

$=\underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{lim}\frac{n}{n(1+\frac{1}{n})}=1$
